articles.title: International Seaways seals $370m Bruton takeover deal
articles.summary: New York-listed tanker owner International Seaways has struck a deal to take over Tor Olav Trøim-backed Bruton in a transaction valuing the Oslo-listed VLCC company at around $370m. articles.body: Americas Europe Tankers International Seaways seals $370m Bruton takeover deal Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 227 3 minutes read Bruton Bruton New York-listed tanker owner International Seaways has struck a deal to take over Tor Olav Trøim-backed Bruton in a transaction valuing the Oslo-listed VLCC company at around $370m. The agreement, announced on Friday, will see the Lois Zabrocky-led group acquire Bruton’s entire four-ship supertanker portfolio, going considerably further than the sale of two newbuildings first linked to the US owner in market reports last week. International Seaways has secured agreements with shareholders representing 50.5% of Bruton, including Trøim’s Drew Holdings and Koch Inc, to exchange their holdings for newly issued shares in the US company. The exchange is set at 0.0519 International Seaways shares for each Bruton share, with the initial transaction expected to settle around October 20. The remaining shares will be acquired through a merger, with Seaways expecting to issue approximately 3.12m new shares, accounting for 96% of the total consideration. Smaller Bruton shareholders will receive cash at $6.3044 per share. The deal brings four 300,000 dwt VLCCs into the Seaways fold, including the LNG dual-fuel Mount Vision , which entered service in July, and sistership Mount Horizon , scheduled for delivery from China’s New Times Shipbuilding next month. The remaining two vessels, Mount Frontier and Mount Summit , are due in August and October 2027. The first two ships already have substantial charter cover. Mount Vision secured a 3+1+1-year arrangement with a trading house, earning $95,000 per day for the initial nine months before switching to an index-linked structure. Mount Horizon has been fixed for 12 to 15 months at $105,700 per day. The two 2027 newbuildings remain unchartered and have been at the centre of the recent sale speculation. Splash detailed the potential deal last week after Bruton acknowledged market rumours and launched a strategic review. At the time, International Seaways was linked to the purchase of at least two newbuildings, with brokers discussing values north of $200m per vessel. Bruton’s own figures put the original yard cost of the two 2027 ships at about $117m apiece, highlighting how sharply modern VLCC asset values have moved. The $370m announced on Friday, however, represents the valuation of Bruton’s equity rather than the gross value of its vessels. The takeover follows a major restructuring of Trøim’s tanker interests. Bruton originally built up a 12-ship VLCC programme before splitting the business in August, retaining its first four New Times ships and transferring another eight newbuildings into separately listed OMC Tankers. The demerger left Bruton with a concentrated fleet of near-term deliveries, substantial charter cover and financing arrangements with Chinese lessors covering 85% to 90% of construction costs. The eight vessels in OMC Tankers are not part of the International Seaways transaction. For International Seaways, the acquisition continues an aggressive fleet renewal programme that has seen the company dispose of older tonnage while selectively investing in younger ships. The US owner had a fleet of around 70 vessels, including newbuildings, before the deal. It sold seven older tankers, including two VLCCs, earlier this year for more than $216m and has also invested in LR1 newbuildings at South Korea’s K Shipbuilding. The company strengthened its crude tanker trading platform in January by taking full ownership of Tankers International, which subsequently expanded into the suezmax market. The latest acquisition comes against an exceptionally strong earnings backdrop. Alongside the takeover announcement, International Seaways unveiled preliminary third-quarter net income of $340m to $350m, including a roughly $50m gain from the sale of a suezmax. It reported liquidity of approximately $965m at the end of September. The transaction also brings together businesses associated with two familiar names in Norwegian shipping. Family trusts established by John Fredriksen, Trøim’s former longtime business partner, hold a 13.54% stake in International Seaways, according to the latest US regulatory filing. The pair went their separate ways in 2014 after nearly two decades working together. Bruton’s board has unanimously recommended the transaction, with a shareholder vote expected around October 30. Completion is targeted for early November, subject to the necessary approvals, after which Bruton intends to delist from Euronext Growth Oslo. articles.title: Lower emissions do not always signal a more efficient container voyage
articles.summary: Lower total emissions do not necessarily mean that a container ship voyage operated more efficiently, according to a new VesselBot case study examining the relationship between emissions and transported cargo. The analysis compares two voyages performed by the same vessel between Bremerhaven and Norfolk in May and...
articles.body: Lower total emissions do not necessarily mean that a container ship voyage operated more efficiently, according to a new VesselBot case study examining the relationship between emissions and transported cargo. The analysis compares two voyages performed by the same vessel between Bremerhaven and Norfolk in May and July 2026. The May voyage generated 3,104 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent emissions while carrying 2,783 TEUs. This resulted in emissions of 1.12 tonnes of CO₂e per TEU. By comparison, the July voyage produced 2,547 tonnes of CO₂e and transported 2,077 TEUs. Although its total emissions were 557 tonnes lower, its emissions intensity reached 1.23 tonnes of CO₂e per TEU. Consequently, the voyage with the higher absolute emissions transported its cargo more efficiently when emissions were measured against the volume carried. Cargo utilisation shapes voyage emissions efficiency VesselBot said that total CO₂e measures the environmental impact of a voyage but does not indicate how efficiently those emissions were used to transport cargo. To assess voyage emissions efficiency, the company uses Well-to-Wake emissions intensity, measured in grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre. The metric relates emissions to the amount of cargo transported and the distance over which it was carried. According to the case study, the average Well-to-Wake emissions intensity across container ship voyages during the second quarter of 2026 was 231.7 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre. Average emissions amounted to 651.3 tonnes of CO₂e per voyage. VesselBot divided the voyages into six emissions-intensity categories. Voyages in the most efficient category, producing up to 49 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre, generated an average of 1,511 tonnes of CO₂e per voyage. In contrast, voyages in the least efficient category, producing at least 800 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre, emitted an average of 545 tonnes. The most efficient voyages recorded average vessel utilisation of 80% and transported 8,946 TEUs. Average utilisation in the least efficient category fell to 31%, with only 340 TEUs carried. The findings indicate that highly utilised vessels can generate more emissions in absolute terms while distributing those emissions across considerably more transport work. Voyage-level modelling supports accurate comparisons VesselBot noted that emissions-intensity calculations depend on the accuracy of the underlying voyage emissions estimates. Fuel consumption is influenced by vessel characteristics, engine performance, sailing speed, time at sea, port stays and operating conditions. As a result, comparisons based only on voyage distance or general industry averages may not accurately represent individual vessel operations. Combining fuel-consumption modelling with shipment-level cargo data allows emissions to be compared with the transport work delivered by each voyage. According to VesselBot, this approach can help shippers evaluate carriers, services and individual sailings on a more comparable basis. It can also distinguish between a voyage that produces fewer emissions because it transports less cargo and one that genuinely uses fuel more efficiently. The study concludes that absolute emissions and operational efficiency should be treated as separate measures when evaluating the environmental performance of container shipping.

articles.title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
articles.summary: West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the...
articles.body: Africa Dry Cargo West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada Sam Chambers October 16, 2026 0 449 3 minutes read Winning Winning West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the decade, with Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project leading the charge. Crucially for shipowners, the long voyages to China will magnify the impact on vessel demand. “West Africa looks set to remain the fastest growing long-haul source of dry bulk cargo,” Tradeviews stated. The growth is already evident. The five West African exporters covered by the consultancy shipped 160.1m tonnes in their principal trades during the first eight months of this year, up 25% year on year. Liberian iron ore exports nearly doubled to 10.1m tonnes. Tradeviews expects regional exports to reach 267m tonnes next year, with Guinean iron ore shipments climbing to 45m tonnes in 2027 and approximately 112m tonnes by 2030. Bauxite exports, meanwhile, are forecast to retreat from a peak of nearly 194m tonnes this year to 153m tonnes by 2030 as Guinea pushes ahead with domestic alumina processing. A capesize round voyage between Guinea and China takes approximately 78 days, compared with just 29 days on the Australia-China route. Tradeviews calculates that moving a tonne from West Africa consequently absorbs around 2.6 times as much vessel time. On this basis, the consultancy estimates West African trades will require the equivalent of 330 capesizes by 2030, compared with 210 last year. There are, however, already signs that the region’s growth ambitions are running up against freight market realities. In its latest weekly report, BRS Shipbrokers noted that exceptionally high freight rates had priced some higher-cost Guinean bauxite miners out of the export market. Guinea shipped 15.61m tonnes of bauxite in September, down 12% from August, with freight costs at one point accounting for more than half the delivered value of the commodity. The subsequent easing in capesize rates could provide some relief. The C3 benchmark has fallen from $43.43 a tonne in late September to $32.95 on October 12, prompting BRS to suggest Guinean bauxite exports could recover by 5% to 10% month on month during November and December. The broker described the situation as a “test of elasticity” rather than the start of another cargo boom, pointing out that Shandong alumina refineries processing imported ore lost RMB261.8 per tonne in September. SSY has similarly warned that Guinean bauxite exports have retreated from early-September highs, observing that “shipping demand is turning more sensitive to margin levels on the mining side”. Tradeviews did also caution that potential Guinean bauxite export restrictions, Simandou project delays, dedicated ore carriers and the displacement of Australian iron ore shipments could reduce the benefits for the wider capesize market with much of the market increasingly looking like a Chinese conveyor belt. SSY noted in a market report from August that VLOCs of more than 220,000 dwt accounted for nearly half of Simandou shipments during the first half of 2026. More significant for independent owners is what is coming down the slipways. SSY data shows Chinese tonnage accounts for nearly 40% of the current VLOC orderbook, raising questions over how much of Simandou’s enormous prospective tonne-mile demand will ultimately filter through to the conventional capesize spot market. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.body: Outlook & Strategy October 16, 2026 · 51 minutes ago Ithaca Energy seeking new CEO as current announces retirement NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Ithaca Energy UK-headquartered oil & gas operator and producer Ithaca Energy is on the lookout for a new chief executive officer (CEO) as Luciano Vasques is set to leave the company next year. Ithaca Energy reported today, October 16, that its current CEO, Luciano Vasques, had informed the board of his intention to retire from the company by March 31, 2027. The board has already started the process of finding a successor, with a further announcement to be made in due course, allowing for an orderly transition of responsibilities. “Following successful delivery of the Business Combination, our entry into the FTSE 100 and the establishment of a strong platform for future growth, I believe the Company is in excellent shape and that now is the right time for me to retire and hand over the reins. I look forward to supporting an orderly transition and watching Ithaca continue to thrive,” Vasques said. Vasques joined Ithaca Energy in October 2024 as CEO, after having held the role of Managing Director of Eni UK Limited and leading the acquisition and integration of Eni Energy UK, formerly Neptune Energy, into Eni UK’s operations. Prior to this, he held the role of Head of Central Asia for Eni S.p.A., overseeing interests in the Kashagan and Karachaganak oil & gas fields. Yaniv Friedman , Executive Chairman, said: “I would like to share my thanks to Luciano for his support during what has been a transformational time for the Company, including the successful integration of Eni UK. articles.title: ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation
articles.summary: ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind...
articles.body: Subsea October 16, 2026 · 1 hour ago ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email ScottishPower Renewables ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind farm in the UK, installing two nearly 1.8-kilometer-long ducts beneath the Suffolk coastline and seabed for the project’s export cables. The ducts, each measuring 800 millimeters in diameter, were installed using horizontal directional drilling (HDD), a technique that creates an underground passage without excavating beaches or disturbing the coastline directly. ScottishPower Renewables says the operation involved the world’s longest continuous single sections of extruded polyethylene (PE) ducts and represents the largest electricity transmission landfall of its kind in the UK, based on the combination of duct length and diameter. Manufactured by Pipelife in Norway, the ducts were produced as single uninterrupted lengths, eliminating the need for welded joints. They will provide a protected route for the high-voltage export cables carrying electricity from the offshore wind farm to shore. The landfall works form part of the project’s onshore civil engineering program, led by OCU Group with support from its subsidiary Peter McCormack & Sons. ScottishPower Renewables said the operation also marked a manufacturing record for Pipelife, whose ducts measured approximately 1,793 meters each. “The completion of this colossal HDD, which is three times the length of our other East Anglia projects, is a huge achievement – quite literally – and a major milestone as we progress construction of our third windfarm in the region,” said Ross Ovens , ScottishPower Renewables’ Managing Director for Offshore. “Landfall works are known to be one of the most technically challenging aspects of building an offshore windfarm, but thanks to precision planning and a great partnership with our principal contactor OCU Group and duct manufacturer Pipelife, this programme has well and truly hit the mark – breaking UK and world records in the process.” The milestone comes as East Anglia Two advances towards offshore construction, with the first export cable expected to be installed in summer 2027, and commercial operation targeted for late 2028. The 960 MW offshore wind farm will be built at a site in the southern North Sea, around 33 kilometers off the Suffolk coast at its nearest point, where 64 Siemens Gamesa SG 14-236 DD wind turbines will be installed on monopile foundations. articles.title: ESPO and EFIP introduce green innovation platform for European ports
articles.summary: The European Sea Ports Organisation (ESPO) and the European Federation of Inland Ports (EFIP) have made the Green Innovation Compass available on their websites. The online platform helps maritime and inland ports find practical solutions for greener and more efficient operations. It brings together research, case...
articles.body: The European Sea Ports Organisation (ESPO) and the European Federation of Inland Ports (EFIP) have made the Green Innovation Compass available on their websites. The online platform helps maritime and inland ports find practical solutions for greener and more efficient operations. It brings together research, case studies and experience from port projects across Europe. The platform focuses on technologies that can help ports reduce emissions, improve efficiency and modernise their infrastructure. Helping ports choose new technologies The Green Innovation Compass was developed through MAGPIE, a European research project that brought together ports, companies, researchers and public authorities. The platform covers electrification, alternative fuels, automation, digitalisation and resilience. It explains how different technologies work, where ports can use them and what they need before introducing them. Ports can search for solutions based on their needs, priorities and project timelines. They can also explore examples from other European ports and learn from their experience. The aim is to make information on port innovation easier to find and use. Rather than recommending one solution for every port, the platform helps users compare different options. Encouraging cooperation between ports ESPO and EFIP want the platform to support greater cooperation across Europe’s port sector. Both organisations believe that sharing experience can help ports overcome common challenges. “The Green Innovation Compass allows for inland ports to see what projects others have already realised,” said Turi Fiorito, Director of EFIP. Isabelle Ryckbost, Secretary General of ESPO, also encouraged ports to use the platform and share their knowledge. The Green Innovation Compass will continue to expand as ports and other organisations contribute new projects and examples. The Alliance for Logistics Innovation through Collaboration in Europe (ALICE) will help maintain the platform after the MAGPIE project ends. The platform is available at GreenInnovationCompass.eu .

articles.body: Asia Containers HMM commits $1.6bn to 12 more containerships Sam Chambers October 16, 2026 0 560 1 minute read HMM HMM South Korea’s HMM is pressing ahead with its fleet expansion programme, approving a $1.62bn investment in 12 containerships comprising eight 13,000 teu newbuildings and four smaller vessels. The Seoul-listed carrier’s board approved spending KRW2.168trn ($1.617bn) yesterday, according to a stock exchange filing. The investment includes fresh orders for eight 13,000 teu ships, alongside the acquisition of three 2,800 teu vessels and one 1,700 teu ship through resale transactions involving newbuildings already under construction. The 12 vessels will add a combined 114,100 teu of capacity, with deliveries scheduled to be completed by December 2029. HMM has yet to identify the shipyards responsible for the eight larger vessels or the sellers of the four smaller ships. Propulsion specifications have also not been disclosed. The latest investment follows last year’s KRW4trn ($2.8bn) commitment covering 12 LNG dual-fuel 13,000 teu containerships and two VLCCs, with HD Hyundai and Hanwha Ocean securing the boxship contracts. Under HMM’s business plan through to 2030, the carrier aims to expand its containership fleet to 166 vessels totalling 1.47m teu by the end of the decade, alongside 110 bulk carriers with a combined capacity of 13.52m dwt. articles.body: ID Logistics has opened a new 35,000 sqm logistics centre in Germany, bringing its network in the country to 17 facilities. The site, located at Mittelweserpark in Lower Saxony, began operations in September 2026 and focuses on handling heavy and bulky goods. The opening marks another step in the company’s expansion in Germany. Since 2021, ID Logistics has more than doubled its network, growing from eight to 17 sites. Its German operations now cover 910,000 sqm of logistics space and employ 4,800 people, compared with 2,800 five years ago. New facility strengthens bulky goods operations The new centre consists of three buildings and can accommodate up to 7,000 oversized items weighing as much as 180 kg. It handles products such as household appliances, sofas and leisure equipment. Operations include order preparation, dispatch and cross-docking. According to ID Logistics, orders can be ready for dispatch within two hours of receipt, while cross-docking shipments have a maximum processing time of four hours. The company has invested in 40 material-handling vehicles, including equipment designed for large and heavy products. Once fully operational, the facility will employ 150 people. The opening also brings ID Logistics’ total space dedicated to heavy and bulky goods in Germany to more than 100,000 sqm. Expanding logistics services across Germany ID Logistics has operated in Germany since 2013. Its services cover warehousing, order preparation, sorting and last-mile delivery, which it introduced in 2024. The company is also developing its transport operations, including full truckload (FTL), less-than-truckload (LTL) and distribution services. The new facility builds on experience from the company’s existing 60,000 sqm centre in Göttingen, which has handled heavy and bulky goods since 2018. Before the Mittelweserpark site opened, some employees completed a three-week training programme in Göttingen to prepare for the new operations. The expansion strengthens ID Logistics’ position in the German contract logistics market, particularly in the handling and distribution of large consumer goods.

articles.body: Europe Greater China Shipyards Tankers Liquimar lines up suezmax trio at New Hantong Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 59 1 minute read Liquimar Liquimar Greek tanker owner Liquimar Tankers has been linked to an order for three suezmax newbuildings in China, adding fresh crude carrier capacity after cashing in on the strong secondhand tanker market. The Dimitris Papadimitriou-controlled company has contracted three 157,000 dwt vessels at Jiangsu New Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, according to shipbuilding sources. The conventionally fuelled tankers are scheduled for delivery in the second half of 2030, with pricing estimated at just under $86m apiece, putting the potential investment at close to $258m. The move follows Liquimar’s disposal of two ageing suezmaxes, the 2007-built Orpheas and Evridiki , to Dubai-based energy trader Onex DMCC. The pair changed hands for a reported $68m each, generating approximately $136m in gross sale proceeds. Both transactions were recorded in September market data. Liquimar has already emerged behind another Chinese tanker project this year. In August, shipbuilding intelligence identified the company as the owner of the 113,500 dwt aframax/LR2 Priamos under construction at Hengli Heavy Industries. That vessel marked the Athens-based owner’s return to newbuilding activity after a lengthy absence. Liquimar was set up in 1990, as a way for its parent company, Dioryx Maritime Corp, to expand from dry cargo and containerships into the oil tanker sector, before becoming a standalone entity in 1995. articles.body: DHL Freight has introduced the SuperPanther eTopas 600 electric truck into regular commercial operations in the Netherlands. The vehicle also serves cross-border routes to Belgium, marking its move from testing to daily freight transport. The battery-electric heavy-duty truck has been operating since September 2026. It covers around 2,000 kilometers per week and offers a range of up to 500 kilometers on a single charge. Unlike vehicles assigned to fixed routes, the eTopas 600 operates across different parts of DHL Freight’s network. This allows the company to assess how electric trucks perform under changing transport requirements. From testing to commercial operations The deployment follows a series of trials carried out by DHL Freight and SuperPanther. The companies began working together in September 2024, before testing the vehicle in Austria earlier this year. During a two-week trial in spring 2026, the truck covered approximately 1,900 kilometers. The first European-built eTopas 600 was completed in July and entered commercial service two months later. According to DHL Freight, initial operating results have been positive, with the truck meeting its planned transport requirements. “Our experience from daily operations has been positive so far. The vehicle meets the requirements of the planned deployment profiles and achieves high productivity within the network,” said Arjan van Weelden, Carrier & Sustainability Manager at DHL Freight Netherlands. DHL plans further electric fleet expansion DHL Freight plans to add around 40 electric trucks to its fleet over the coming months. The company is using data from the eTopas 600 to assess how battery-electric vehicles can support regular freight operations, including international routes. “Our customers are looking for practical ways to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from their transport operations,” said Heidi van Eldik, CEO of DHL Freight Netherlands & Belgium. DHL Freight currently operates around 1,700 vehicles designed to reduce transport emissions. The company is also testing different vehicle technologies as part of DHL Group’s target to achieve net-zero emissions in logistics by 2050.

articles.title: Shipping’s AI winners will build capability, not buy technology
articles.summary: The technology is already widely available. The advantage will come from how shipping companies turn it into specialised systems, define its place in the team and manage adoption, says Michalis Gkontas, co-founder and CEO of AskChief. Today’s AI systems can already perform useful knowledge work. They can search and...
articles.body: Operations Tech Shipping’s AI winners will build capability, not buy technology Splash October 16, 2026 0 47 3 minutes read Gerd Altmann via Pixabay Gerd Altmann via Pixabay The technology is already widely available. The advantage will come from how shipping companies turn it into specialised systems, define its place in the team and manage adoption, says Michalis Gkontas, co-founder and CEO of AskChief. Today’s AI systems can already perform useful knowledge work. They can search and interpret large volumes of information, compare documents, prepare drafts and help people work through complex tasks. The more important question now is whether organisations are ready to deploy them well. Giving employees access to a general-purpose AI tool is easy. Turning that access into better technical work, stronger compliance and additional team capacity is a management challenge. Leaders must decide where AI should be used, what knowledge it can draw on and where professional responsibility remains. Access is not capability As connectivity improves across fleets, many seafarers can access the same general-purpose AI tools as colleagues ashore, whether or not their company has formally deployed them. A report or proposed response may arrive in polished language without showing what evidence supports it, which company procedure applies or how much was generated by AI. Fluent output is not necessarily useful output. Generic AI can make weak reasoning look convincing or produce material that does not fit the vessel’s actual circumstances. The shore team must then reconstruct the context and verify the basis of what it has received. A generic model does not naturally know which version of a company’s safety management system is current, whether a manual applies to the equipment fitted on a particular vessel or who must approve a proposed SMS change. Specialisation comes from the system built around the model: the company’s knowledge, role-specific instructions, specialist tools, established workflows, permissions and review points. The underlying model may be general-purpose. The operational system should not be. Begin with work that matters The weakest deployment brief is simply to “use AI more”. It leaves each employee to decide what the technology is for, which information is appropriate to use and how much confidence to place in the result. A stronger starting point is a recurring piece of work the team already understands: investigating a technical issue, preparing for an inspection, answering an SMS question or assessing how a new requirement affects company procedures. The task should be meaningful enough to matter but bounded enough to manage. Once the team sees AI supporting a familiar workflow, expansion becomes an operational decision rather than an abstract technology initiative. Let AI do the work around the decision AI is well suited to locating relevant material, assembling context, comparing records, identifying potential gaps and preparing a first draft. People remain responsible for interpreting the evidence, challenging its relevance, resolving uncertainty and approving the action. Its purpose is not to diminish professional expertise, but to extend its reach. A useful shorthand is the 10-80-10 rule. It is not a literal allocation of time or effort, but a sequence for organising the work. In the first 10%, the expert defines the problem, supplies the context and sets the standard for a good outcome. AI carries much of the middle 80% by finding information, structuring it, comparing records and preparing the work. In the final 10%, the accountable professional challenges the result, corrects it and decides what happens next. The percentages should change with the risk. A safety-critical decision may require far more human review than a routine summary. Make adoption a team practice Leaders need to set expectations, appoint owners and create simple feedback loops. Teams should be able to share useful cases, flag weak outputs, and show where information or workflow design needs improvement. In shipping, caution is usually rational. A confident but incorrect answer can waste time or introduce risk. Trust grows when users can inspect the underlying evidence, understand the system’s boundaries and see that their professional judgement remains central. The same discipline should shape measurement. Logins and prompts reveal little. Better questions are whether the team reached a reviewed outcome faster, used relevant company history, avoided duplicate work and captured the decision for the next person. Deployment will create the advantage AI models will keep becoming more powerful and widely available. Access will not be scarce, and it will not provide a durable advantage on its own. The difference will come from deployment: choosing the right work, building specialised systems around it and helping teams incorporate those systems into everyday operations. For leaders, this means treating AI neither as a standalone IT purchase nor as an instruction to reduce headcount. It is an opportunity to give capable people better tools and increase what the organisation can accomplish without weakening accountability. The technology exists. The management challenge is to turn it into a working organisational capability. The shipping companies that do this well will not simply have more people using AI. They will have better-equipped teams, stronger company knowledge and more capacity to act. articles.body: Europe Offshore Former Ukrainian officer goes on trial over Nord Stream sabotage Bojan Lepic October 16, 2026 0 84 1 minute read Swedish Coast Guard Swedish Coast Guard Germany has opened its first criminal trial over the 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, with a former Ukrainian military officer accused of leading the team that carried out the explosions in the Baltic Sea. German prosecutors accuse 50-year-old Serhii Kuznietsov of involvement in a war crime through an attack on civilian infrastructure, as well as causing an explosion, destroying infrastructure, and disrupting public services. Kuznietsov did not testify on the opening day, while his defence sought to have the proceedings dismissed. Prosecutors allege he led a group that travelled aboard the sailing yacht Andromeda, rented in Rostock using false documentation, before divers placed explosives on the pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm. Investigators believe specialised explosives fitted with timers were attached to the pipelines on the seabed. The blasts on September 26, 2022, ruptured three of the four Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipeline strings, triggering large gas leaks in the Baltic. The pipeline system was built to transport Russian gas directly to Germany. Nord Stream 1 had capacity to carry around 55 bn cu m annually, but Russia had halted flows before the explosions. Nord Stream 2 was completed in 2021 but never entered commercial operation after Germany suspended its certification shortly before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Responsibility for the attack has been disputed for four years. Ukraine has denied involvement, while Russia has rejected allegations that it carried out the sabotage and has accused Western countries of involvement, claims they deny. German investigators have meanwhile pursued several Ukrainian suspects. A second man, alleged to have been one of the divers involved in placing the explosives, was arrested in Croatia in August. articles.body: Fincantieri is accelerating the use of artificial intelligence and robotics across its shipyards through its BOOST² innovation programme. The initiative includes planned investments of nearly €100 million to improve shipbuilding efficiency, safety and production processes. The Italian shipbuilding group launched BOOST² – The Shipyard of the Future three years ago. Since then, more than 450 employees across 13 shipyards have taken part in the programme, including teams in Italy, Romania and the United States. Fincantieri presented its latest progress at the Castellammare di Stabia shipyard on 13 October. The demonstrations included technologies already in use, systems undergoing testing and solutions being developed for future operations. Bringing AI and robotics into shipbuilding The programme focuses on moving new technologies from testing into regular shipyard operations. One of its main areas is Physical AI, which allows intelligent systems to interact with machinery and their surroundings. Fincantieri is also developing collaborative robots to support workers during complex production tasks. Other technologies include digital twins, which create digital models of shipyard assets and processes, and smart supply chain systems designed to improve production planning and coordination. The company is also exploring additive manufacturing and automated industrial equipment. To support these developments, Fincantieri works with technology companies, startups and research partners. The aim is to adapt new solutions to shipbuilding requirements before introducing them across more facilities. Expanding technology across the shipyard network Fincantieri is now focusing on wider adoption of technologies that have already shown promising results. “The next frontier of industrial competitiveness is bringing artificial intelligence into the physical world, integrating it with robotics and the expertise embedded in our manufacturing operations,” said Pierroberto Folgiero, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director of Fincantieri. The company plans to continue testing new applications while expanding the use of existing systems. It also aims to strengthen cooperation between engineering, production and technology teams. Through BOOST², Fincantieri is seeking to make automation and digital technologies a regular part of its shipbuilding operations.

articles.title: Sea-Intelligence: Liner Networks Getting More Specialized
articles.summary: The global container shipping industry is undergoing a structural transformation, with shipping lines transitioning away from the highly homogenized networks of the past decade toward a landscape characterized by greater operational specialization. Prior to 2017, the deep‑sea network was heavily consolidated. To...
articles.body: The global container shipping industry is undergoing a structural transformation, with shipping lines transitioning away from the highly homogenized networks of the past decade toward a landscape characterized by greater operational specialization. Prior to 2017, the deep‑sea network was heavily consolidated. To maintain global market coverage, shipping lines relied extensively on dense Vessel Sharing Agreements (VSAs) to pool capacity. This operational strategy created a deeply homogenized market, wherein the same physical service was marketed under multiple brand names by different shipping lines, creating an illusion of choice for shippers. Recent years point to a stark divergence between the physical expansion of liner networks and the contraction of commercial offerings. While the underlying physical network has expanded from roughly 250 active deep‑sea services in 2012‑2013 to nearly 380 by late 2026, the number of shipping lines actively offering space across these services has steadily declined. This shifting dynamic is most clearly illustrated by Figure 1, which calculates the average density of vessel sharing in the market. Source: Sea-Intelligence.com, Sunday Spotlight, issue 786 During the peak of market homogenization in 2014‑2016, the average liner service was a highly shared asset. A single physical liner service was offered as a product by an average of 4.12 shipping lines. By August 2026, this multiplier has dropped to just 2.65, showing that shipping lines are demonstrably reducing their reliance on shared capacity and are instead increasingly choosing to shoulder more of the operational risk individually. Consequently, physical routing options are becoming increasingly distinct, signalling the return of true operational competition in the market.

Cunnion helped design the new business plan and company framework, oversaw the implementation of a new customer-first operation and reduced supply chain costs by 21 percent. Cunnion is a graduate of Nichols College, where he received Bachelor of Science in Business Administration, Double Major in Economics and Finance. He also was an officer in the U.S Army, rising to the rank of Captain and receiving two Bronze Star Medals during deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. He serves on the board of the Foreign Commerce Club of Boston and the Sharon Cooperative & Nature School. He is also involved with industry associations such as the Northeast Association of Rail Shippers, the Coalition of New England Companies for Trade and the International Forest Products Transport Association. The Port of Boston generates $8.2 billion in annual economic impact and supports more than 66,000 jobs. Keeping the Port competitive to generate future economic growth and support job creation is an essential part of the Authority’s mission. As Port Director, Cunnion will lead Massport's Maritime Division. “Charlie is an expert in supply chain management, with decades of experience across all modes of cargo transportation,” said Massport CEO Rich Davey. “His leadership, experience and strategic perspective will be invaluable to the Port of Boston as we work to strengthen operations and continue a tradition of innovation and growth. I am thrilled to have him on my leadership team and look forward to seeing him build on the success of Conley Terminal and Flynn Cruiseport in his new role.” Conley Container Terminal enables more than 2,500 businesses throughout Massachusetts and New England to ship and receive products globally, including furniture and home goods, footwear, clothing, office supplies, wine and spirits, recycled fibers, sporting goods, seafood and more. With over 454,000 passengers and 149 ship calls in 2025, Flynn Cruiseport helped boost economic activity and tourism in the Commonwealth, generating $256 million annually in economic impact and creating over 3,000 jobs. Nearly 80 percent of the ships that currently serve Boston can plug into shore power or use alternative low-carbon technology. When ships use shore power, they tap landside electricity for their power needs at berth including lights, pumps, communications, and refrigeration, instead of running diesel-fueled auxiliary on-board engines.

articles.body: Maritime piracy incidents remain at historic lows despite Somali piracy concerns in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 The ICC International Maritime Bureau (IMB) has reported the lowest level (51) of piracy and armed robbery incidents since 1992 in the first nine months of 2026. However, a recent resurgence of Somali piracy incidents highlights the continued risks facing seafarers, with IMB urging vigilance, timely reporting and strict adherence to Best Management Practices (BMP). The IMB Piracy Reporting Centre (PRC) reported 51 incidents for the period of January-September 2026, down from 116 in the same period last year, the lowest reported nine-month figures since 1992. The report reveals that 36 vessels were boarded, eight hijacked, four fired upon and three attempted boardings. In 86% of incidents, perpetrators successfully gained access to the vessel while either at anchor or steaming with most boarding incidents occurring at night. The threat of violence against crew remains a concern, with 105 crew directly affected, compared to 72 in the same period in 2025. Weapons were identified in 53% of reported incidents in the first nine months of 2026. IMB Director Michael Howlett said: “While incident levels are at their lowest in more than three decades, the recent uptick in Somali piracy activity is a reminder that the threat remains. Incidents this year have also shown that strict adherence to BMP recommendations remains one of the most effective ways to deter hijacking attempts and protect crews. Continued vigilance is essential to safeguarding seafarers and the vital trade routes on which the global economy depends.” Somali piracy risks heighten While overall piracy incidents remain at historic lows, IMB recorded a rise in Somali piracy activity from January to September 2026, with Somali pirates responsible for eight vessel hijackings and 94% of all crew taken hostage globally. Most hijacked vessels have been released with the crew reported safe. IMB notes that vessels implementing the latest BMP have continued to successfully deter hijacking attempts, even in cases where pirates have managed to board a vessel. However, Puntland authorities reported in late September that five crew members were killed and five injured prior to the release of the Palau-flagged product tanker Honour 25, hijacked on 21 April 2026. While these incidents highlight the continued capability of Somali pirates to target vessels in the region, they are not comparable in scale or reach to the deep-sea piracy operations that characterised the 2008-2013 Somali piracy era. Declining incidents in the Gulf of Guinea and the Singapore Straits Two incidents were reported from January to September 2026 in the Gulf of Guinea waters with none in the last quarter. The IMB commends the littoral states of the Gulf of Guinea for their continued efforts in ensuring incidents of piracy and armed robbery remain at these low levels. Similarly, there has been a welcome reduction in reported incidents in the Singapore Straits, with 13 in the first nine months of 2026 compared to 73 during the same period in 2025. Two crew were taken hostage and a further two were threatened and one was injured in 2026 in the Singapore Straits. In over 69% of incidents perpetrators were armed with either guns or knives and managed to successfully board all targeted vessels indicating the continued risk to shipping in these waters. IMB commends the actions of the authorities which have contributed to the reduction in reported incidents in the Singapore Straits. Reduced levels of reported incidents in the Indonesian Archipelagic continues. Six incidents were reported in the first nine months of 2026 compared to nine during the same period in 2025. Weapons were reported in one incident in which one crew was also taken hostage. Nine anchored vessels were boarded in the Philippines, with six incidents reported in Manila and three in Batangas, compared to no reported incidents in 2025. Two crew members were taken hostage during the incidents, while weapons were reported in five cases. “The drop in reported incidents in the Gulf of Guinea and Singapore Straits is encouraging and reflects the positive impact of sustained efforts by the authorities. It is important to maintain this momentum through continued vigilance and timely reporting of all incidents,” said Mr Howlett. articles.summary: Tanker supply has been growing over the past few years, as more and more newbuildings are entering the global fleet. articles.body: Tanker Rates Are Up, But So Is Ships’ Supply in Hellenic Shipping News 16/10/2026 T anker supply has been growing over the past few years, as more and more newbuildings are entering the global fleet. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “tanker fleet growth has accelerated considerably over the past two years, marking a clear shift from the unusually restrained supply environment that supported the market earlier in the cycle. Across the main tanker segments, combined fleet capacity has increased from approximately 677.8 mills DWT at the end of 2023 to around 738.9 mills DWT currently, representing growth of roughly 9.0%. However, the expansion has been far from uniform. Small tankers, MR2s and Aframax/LR2s have recorded the strongest capacity growth since end-2023, increasing by approximately 15.3%, 13.8% and 14.3%, respectively. By contrast, VLCC/ULCC capacity has expanded by only around 4.2%, while Handy/MR1 growth has remained similarly limited”. Source: Xclusiv According to Xclusiv, “the pace of additions has nevertheless changed sharply. Deliveries across the tanker fleet totalled only around 7.6 mills DWT in 2024 before rising to approximately 19.5 mills DWT in 2025. During 2026 to date, around 32.6 mills DWT has already entered the fleet, highlighting the extent to which the newbuilding cycle has begun translating into physical supply. MR2 and Aframax/LR2 deliveries have been particularly substantial, while the larger crude tanker segments are now also seeing a notable increase. VLCC/ULCC deliveries, for example, have risen from just one vessel in 2024 and six in 2025 to 31 vessels during 2026 so far. More importantly, the delivery pipeline remains heavy beyond the current year. The tanker orderbook has expanded substantially across almost every segment compared with end-2023. The most pronounced exposure is now concentrated among the larger crude carriers: the current Suezmax orderbook stands at approximately 29.6% of the existing fleet in DWT terms, while VLCC/ULCC has climbed to around 32.5%. Aframax/LR2 and MR2 orderbooks are also significant at approximately 20.7% and 19.7%, respectively. This represents a very different supply backdrop from only a few years ago, particularly for VLCCs, where limited ordering had previously kept forward fleet growth exceptionally low. Scheduled 2027 deliveries amount to approximately 50.7 mills DWT, equivalent to almost 6.9% of the current tanker fleet. The delivery profile becomes heavier again in 2028, with around 61.2 mills DWT currently scheduled, while a further 67.5 mills DWT sits in the 2029-and-beyond pipeline. On headline numbers alone, this creates clear supply-side pressure, raises the importance of demand growth, slippage and recycling in determining how much of this capacity ultimately translates into effective fleet expansion”. The shipbroker added that “the age profile offers an important counterbalance. Around 19.8% of the current tanker fleet by vessel count is already more than 20 years old, while almost half is above 15 years. The replacement requirement is particularly pronounced in Handy/MR1 and Panamax/LR1, where approximately 37.3% and 22.6% of vessels, respectively, are over 20 years old. Even within the larger crude tanker segments, close to one-fifth of Aframax/LR2 and VLCC/ULCC vessels are already above the 20-year threshold. A heavier delivery program could therefore coincide with greater recycling and replacement of ageing tonnage rather than translate entirely into incremental effective supply. Demand growth, however, appears comparatively limited on the current forecasts. Total seaborne oil trade is projected at around 62.8m bpd in 2027, slightly below the 63.4m bpd recorded in 2025. Within that, crude oil trade is expected to edge higher to approximately 40.7m bpd, while oil products remain below 2025 levels. As a result, simple volume growth may not be sufficient to absorb the incoming fleet”. Source: Xclusiv “The tanker market is therefore moving into a more supply-sensitive phase. The key question for 2027 and beyond will not simply be how many vessels are delivered, but how effectively ageing tonnage exits the trading fleet and how geopolitical developments, trade dislocations and changing sourcing patterns affect tonne-mile demand. With a significantly larger orderbook now approaching delivery, vessel utilization and trade distances will become increasingly important in determining whether headline fleet growth translates into genuine oversupply”, Xclusiv concluded. articles.title: MR Freight Divergence: A Market Poised for Rebalancing
articles.summary: MR demand shifts back towards regional trading Pacific origin MR earnings have maintained a substantial premium over Atlantic routes throughout 2026, while regional tonne mile demand has shifted considerably since April as trade patterns adjusted to disruptions in the Middle East Gulf. Following the disruption, MR...
articles.body: MR Freight Divergence: A Market Poised for Rebalancing in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 M R demand shifts back towards regional trading Pacific origin MR earnings have maintained a substantial premium over Atlantic routes throughout 2026, while regional tonne mile demand has shifted considerably since April as trade patterns adjusted to disruptions in the Middle East Gulf. Following the disruption, MR vessels ballasted from the Pacific into the Atlantic in search of alternative employment, subsequently undertaking longer Atlantic to Pacific voyages. This temporarily lifted Atlantic origin tonne mile demand to an April peak, while Pacific demand declined sharply. As trade patterns adjusted, these exceptional voyages gradually subsided and MR employment became more regionalised. Atlantic origin tonne miles declined from their April peak, while Pacific demand recovered on stronger exports from India and Northeast Asia. By July, tonne mile demand across the two basins had largely converged, reversing the initial imbalance caused by the disruption. Changing trade patterns underpin Pacific MR demand Pacific MR tonne mile recovery has been driven by stronger exports from India’s west coast and Northeast Asia, helping offset the substantial decline in Middle East Gulf loadings. Longer shipments towards the west coast of South America and southern and eastern Africa have provided additional vessel employment, supporting tonne mile demand beyond the growth in cargo volumes alone. Indian refiners have maintained throughput by diversifying crude sourcing and drawing on inventories, sustaining product exports despite disruptions to traditional Middle East supplies. Similarly, Chinese refiners have tapped crude inventories to mitigate feedstock shortages. China’s diesel exports subsequently reached a four year high in September, generating 29 MR voyages predominantly towards Southeast Asia and Oceania. Oceania remains an important source of underlying Pacific MR demand, supported by Australia’s structural reliance on imported refined products following domestic refinery closures. Continued CPP imports, particularly from Asian suppliers, provide relatively stable regional employment, complementing the growth in longer distance shipments from India and Northeast Asia. In contrast, Atlantic origin tonne miles have weakened as Baltic exports declined. Strong intra Mediterranean CPP activity has provided some replacement employment, but shorter voyage distances have limited its contribution to tonne mile demand. Meanwhile, reduced Russian diesel supplies to Brazil have been partly replaced by US Gulf exports. Although this has supported US Gulf MR employment, the additional voyages have not fully compensated for lost Baltic tonne miles. Russian diesel recovery and Asian refinery activity shape the demand outlook US government’s recent announcement of a deal with Russia to supply the global diesel market raises the prospect of recovering Russian exports, but an immediate rebound remains unlikely given uncertainty over refinery capacity. Although attacks on Russian refineries have been limited over the past two months, it remains unclear whether refinery throughput can return to 2025 levels. Any recovery in exports is therefore likely to be gradual, with additional volumes initially favouring shorter Mediterranean voyages before longer shipments towards South America recover. A return of Russian diesel to Brazil could also displace US Gulf cargoes, limiting the net increase in Atlantic MR tonne mile demand. In the Pacific, Chinese clean product exports face a weaker outlook following September’s 36 month high of 3.9mt. China’s final export quota allocation fell to 4.55mt from 8.4mt last year, bringing the annual total 11% below 2025 levels. Seaborne exports are expected to moderate from around 2.8mt in October to 2mt per month in November and December. Nevertheless, MR employment could remain more resilient than the decline in aggregate export volumes suggests, particularly if Chinese shipments remain concentrated on shorter routes towards Southeast Asia and Oceania, where MRs account for a substantial share of export voyages. Continued Indian exports towards Africa and South America should also support longer distance MR employment. Growing Pacific MR supply could narrow the earnings differential Stronger Pacific earnings have encouraged MR tonnage to reposition from the Atlantic, reversing the net outflows observed between May and August. With eastward movements increasing while westward flows remain stable, net inflows into the Pacific have reached around 20 vessels, although still below the April peak. This shift comes as Pacific demand faces increasing uncertainty, with Chinese clean product exports expected to moderate towards year end. While resilient Oceania imports and continued exports from India and Northeast Asia should support employment, further vessel inflows could gradually ease Pacific supply tightness. Meanwhile, declining vessel availability in the Atlantic could help support earnings, particularly if Russian diesel exports recover. The resulting supply adjustment across both basins could correct freight in both regions and gradually narrow the Pacific earnings premium towards year end. Source: Vortexa Tops 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

This temporarily lifted Atlantic origin tonne mile demand to an April peak, while Pacific demand declined sharply.
As trade patterns adjusted, these exceptional voyages gradually subsided and MR employment became more regionalised.

articles.title: Xeneta: The End Of Q3 Knocked Global Reliability Down To 27% On-Time As Delay Climbed To 6.0 Days
articles.summary: Global reliability fell for the fourth consecutive month down to 27% on-time, 2pp lower than August and now matching February’s floor earlier in the year. There is little prospect of hitting a firm floor in October given continued deterioration on Asian trades following a sequence of powerful typhoons that landed...
articles.body: Xeneta: The End Of Q3 Knocked Global Reliability Down To 27% On-Time As Delay Climbed To 6.0 Days in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 G lobal reliability fell for the fourth consecutive month down to 27% on-time, 2pp lower than August and now matching February’s floor earlier in the year. There is little prospect of hitting a firm floor in October given continued deterioration on Asian trades following a sequence of powerful typhoons that landed from July through early September. Average vessel delay increased in step, rising for four consecutive months up to a 6.0 day average across all arrivals and a total 2.4 day rise since the beginning of Q2. Trades: Far East to Europe collapsed to 4% on-time as Asia-linked trades hit 12-month lows This month’s trade reliability splits sharply by geography: Asia-linked trades sit at or near 12-month lows of on-time arrivals and 12-month highs on average delay. The compound effect of typhoons on existing constraints insists that the right combination of circumstances can continue to eat away at global reliability months after the fact and far from the original localization. Far East to Europe nose-dived to 4% on-time with a stunning 9.9 days of average delay across all vessels, its worst month since September 2021 when it hit 3% on-time. Far East to North America held flat at 20% on-time while delay rose by 0.8 days from August to a total of 6.9 days in September. Rates are following an equally unfavorable path for shippers. Xeneta’s spot market average for China to US West Coast reached $7,717 per FEU in early October, over four times September 2025 ($1,778) and up 8% on the start of September 2026. Long-term rates are catching up from a much lower base, at $3,649 per FEU on 1 October but rising +26% month on month. As Death by a Thousand Paper Cuts explains, no single factor controls the current climate: bunker costs, ongoing typhoon disruption, and a strong peak season have each added to it. South America West Coast and East Coast were the only trades to improve across both reliability metrics this past month, gaining +10pp and +12pp respectively and cutting average delay by up to 1.0 day. It’s a positive streak in what feels like an uncompromising environment, and good timing as there is little slack left to absorb delays going into Brazil’s peak export season. On the upper end of the spectrum, Europe to North America led for the second month running, outpacing South America West Coast on +8pp MoM improvement to 49% on-time – its highest since August 2025 – and the lowest average delay of any trade at 1.9 days. Carriers: Every carrier posted a 12-month delay high as shippers prepare for tenders Every carrier posted its highest average delay over the past 12 months in September, but only four hit a 12-month low in on-time arrivals: CMA CGM (30%), Cosco (18%), Hapag-Lloyd (45%) and Yang Ming (4%). The increased risk lies in severity rather than the frequency of late arrivals. Buffer days in contracts and inventory plans are being consumed at an alarming rate, and the ongoing deterioration means any contingency plans set in motion today may not hold up when your next booking arrives. The spread between carriers continues to compress, from 45pp in August to 43pp this month. While the on-time floor fell as Yang Ming hit 4%, the ceiling came down as Maersk fell from 51% to 47%. Leaders are falling as opposed to underperformers catching up; holding carriers charging a premium for service reliability accountable is a must for shippers going into 2027 tenders. Both Gemini partners have declined MoM for the past five months, and the Gemini network has fallen harder than other alliances, from 70% on-time in June to 40% in September. A weekly perspective shows how severely the tail-end of typhoon delays stacked up out of Asia: from 62% in the first week of August down to 34% by the week of 28 September. Port Congestion: Singapore’s queue doubles as Chinese port delays spill into Southeast Asia’s transshipment hub Average vessel wait times in Africa’s ports fell by nearly a full day to 2.5 days in September, and the share of vessels waiting held at 32%, yet the region still leads global congestion. Apart from a modest 0.1-day dip in Northern Europe, Africa was the only region to improve. Southeast Asia follows at 2.0 days of average vessel wait, edging past the Middle East, with the share of vessels waiting increasing up to 23%. Vessel queues in Singapore nearly doubled from 12 to 22 vessels per day at 29% and average wait spiked from 1.9 to 3.1 days as it continued to absorb downstream effects from Chinese port congestion. The Middle East held flat across both vessel wait times at 1.9 days and the share of vessels waiting at 26%. Smaller gateways such as Sohar continue to feel the strain of functioning as pressure valves for the Strait of Hormuz, absorbing over 180,000 in displaced weekly TEU and less than half of the 423,000 TEU bound for Jebel Ali before the war. In Northeast Asia, just under a third of vessels at port were waiting in September at 30%, and average wait rose by 0.3 days to 1.6 days total. Waits were shorter than leading congestion in Africa and Southeast Asia, but pressure from the late-summer typhoons and pre-Golden Week demand kept space tight and yards utilization high. Queues remain long at Chinese ports, and they show up as increasingly severe berth-arrival delays for shippers in North America and Europe. Shanghai is one exception, where the queue shortened from 101 to 86 vessels at anchorage on an average day and wait lengthened from 1.9 to 2.7 days. A short average wait can still hide a long queue and a long wait can sit behind a short one, so shippers should check queue length and wait severity together when assessing congestion impact on their bookings. Special: Blanks eased in September but carriers are ramping back up With so much capacity absorbed by delays in September bunching up against pre-Golden Week demand, carriers blanked just 6% of planned capacity on Far East to Europe, the third-lowest share of the past 21 months. On Far East to North America it was 8%, also the third-lowest in the same period. That said, blanking is stepping up sharply in October to at least 17% of planned capacity on Far East to Europe and 13% on Far East to North America. The announced share is still below October 2025, which could mean carriers are keeping more capacity in rotation to work off the typhoon backlog, or that more cancellations will land in the following weeks. Planned capacity on Far East to Europe in October is the highest of any month in a 22-month window, and Far East to North America’s is third-highest. With more capacity scheduled into Golden Week and a smaller cut compared to 2025, a trade hitting 4% on-time has even less slack to offset delays with voided sailings. For shippers in Europe and North America, that means October bookings should be given more lead time and carriers should be asked which services they are protecting from capacity cuts. What to watch • Gemini has not found a floor. The network’s weekly on-time rate has fallen sharply since early August, and the week of 5 October already reads 28% on partial data. A network with no slack between disruptions may mean Gemini’s reliability advantage over competitors faces a longer road to recovery. • Chinese anchorages are clearing, but the disruption is moving downstream, not disappearing. Ningbo and Yantian waits eased in the same month Far East to Europe hit 4%, and the delay is landing at berths in Europe and North America. Shanghai, Ningbo and Yantian still held 0.74 million TEU at anchor as of 6 October. • China to US West Coast spot rates sit at more than twice the long-term rate ($7,717 vs $3,649 per FEU). Contracts are repricing upward, so renewals are likely to cost more, and delays now hit shippers’ budgets as well as their lead times. • Shippers shouldn’t let narratives around port congestion take attention away from carrier accountability. Schedule reliability, port rotations and unscheduled calls, and how much capacity is deliberately cut, shape the price and downstream cost of a booking just as much as port performance. Know which services deliver before you sign With Far East to Europe at 4% on-time and a 43pp spread across carriers, the tender decisions you make now depend on knowing which services actually deliver. Xeneta Ocean Schedules gives you port pair, service and carrier reliability data, updated monthly, so you can benchmark your lanes before you commit. articles.title: New BIMCO contracts tackle ship recycling and energy-saving retrofits
articles.summary: We have adopted two new contractual solutions designed to help you manage important operational and regulatory challenges: the revised RECYCLECON contract and the Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum 2026. Practical frameworks for recycling and retrofits At its online meeting on 8 October, our Documentary Committee...
articles.body: New BIMCO contracts tackle ship recycling and energy-saving retrofits in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 We have adopted two new contractual solutions designed to help you manage important operational and regulatory challenges: the revised RECYCLECON contract and the Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum 2026. Practical frameworks for recycling and retrofits At its online meeting on 8 October, our Documentary Committee adopted the revised RECYCLECON* contract. It gives you a modern contractual framework for the sale of ships for safe and environmentally sound recycling, reflecting the requirements and principles of the Hong Kong Convention. It also updates the commercial and documentary arrangements between sellers, buyers and recycling facilities. The revision comes at an important time, as so many ships are expected to reach the end of their operational lives in the coming years. The committee also adopted the Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum 2026. If you own or charter ships, the addendum gives you a flexible framework for agreeing how to allocate the costs, time and benefits involved in fitting energy-saving equipment during a time charter. Responding to sanctions and electric vehicle risks The committee discussed a proposed EU Tanker Sale and Resale Restrictions Clause in response to EU sanctions affecting tanker sales. As sanctions become more frequent and complex, we are working to provide clauses that turn regulatory requirements into practical, balanced contractual provisions you can use. It also considered the proposed Clause for the Carriage of Electric Vehicles. This work reflects the growing number of new and used electric vehicles carried by sea, as well as the increased focus on the related safety, operational and commercial considerations. Modernising the heavy-lift framework We are continuing to revise HEAVYLIFTVOY, our voyage charter party for the mid-sized heavy-lift sector. The form is relevant if you carry specialist or project cargo on or under deck, particularly in the lift-on/lift-off and roll-on/roll-off markets. The revision is focusing on loading and discharge, notice of readiness, laytime, detention and waiting time. We are also revising the accompanying bill of lading and developing a new sea waybill to give you greater flexibility. Supporting digital trade and more efficient voyages Digitalisation remains central to our work. The committee reviewed the revision of the Electronic Bills of Lading Clause 2014, building on our efforts to help the industry move away from paper documentation. The revised clause is intended to reflect current legislation and market practice, support the growing use of electronic bills of lading and remain flexible enough for further technological development, including interoperability between electronic systems. Digital tools can also support more efficient vessel operations. Our proposed Just in Time Arrival and Virtual Notice of Readiness Clause will allow owners and charterers to agree speed adjustments so that a vessel meets an agreed arrival time. For ports supporting the approach, the intention is that a vessel will be able to tender virtual notice of readiness before reaching the contractual loading or discharging place. Together, these mechanisms are intended to improve voyage and arrival planning, reduce unnecessary waiting at or near ports, and create opportunities to save fuel and reduce emissions. All while maintaining a practical and balanced allocation of contractual rights and obligations. Developing the first dedicated offshore wind installation contract Work is also progressing on WINDSEACON, the first dedicated BIMCO standard contract for the transport and installation of offshore wind turbines. The offshore wind market has often relied on a mixture of construction contracts and amended offshore charter forms, which can lead to lengthy negotiations and contractual uncertainty. WINDSEACON is intended to give you a balanced and commercially practical framework tailored to offshore wind projects. It aims to improve efficiency, reduce transaction costs, clarify risk allocation and support continued investment in renewable energy infrastructure. Our dedicated subcommittee is meeting regularly throughout 2026 to refine the draft and address the complex commercial, operational and risk-allocation issues involved in transporting and installing offshore wind turbines. articles.title: LR launches new guidance to help shipowners navigate the growing complexity of retrofit projects
articles.summary: New guidance highlights the practical challenges shipowners face as they retrofit existing vessels for alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies to meet evolving environmental regulations. Lloyd’s Register (LR) has published new Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices...
articles.body: LR launches new guidance to help shipowners navigate the growing complexity of retrofit projects in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 New guidance highlights the practical challenges shipowners face as they retrofit existing vessels for alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies to meet evolving environmental regulations. Lloyd’s Register (LR) has published new Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices highlighting the growing complexity of ship retrofit projects. As regulatory and commercial pressures increase through measures such as FuelEU Maritime, the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) and the IMO’s greenhouse gas reduction ambitions, retrofitting existing vessels is becoming an increasingly important pathway for owners seeking to improve efficiency, reduce emissions and extend asset life. However, the challenge is no longer simply selecting a single fuel or technology. Retrofit projects have become increasingly complex, requiring careful consideration of fuel storage, engine compatibility, safety systems, crew training, statutory approvals, vessel design and long-term operational impacts. To help the industry navigate these challenges, LR’s new publication brings together alternative fuels and energy-saving devices within a single retrofit framework. It covers the practical considerations associated with converting vessels to LNG, methanol, ethanol, ammonia, hydrogen and LPG, alongside the installation of wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS) and air lubrication systems (ALS). A central theme is that many retrofit decisions must be made much earlier in the process than owners may expect. Factors such as engine conversion capability, available onboard space, tank location, fuel-system integration and project execution can have a major influence on project costs, timelines and operational outcomes. The guidance emphasises the importance of early collaboration between owners, shipyards, equipment manufacturers, flag administrations and classification societies to avoid delays and reduce project risk. The publication also highlights growing opportunities for energy-saving technologies. Wind-assisted propulsion systems, for example, can benefit from incentives under FuelEU Maritime through a reward factor designed to recognise their contribution to lowering greenhouse gas intensity At the same time, the guidance notes reflect growing industry recognition that retrofit projects must address both technical and human factors. Extensive crew training, revised operating procedures, updated safety management systems and new risk assessments are identified as essential elements of successful deployment, particularly for fuels such as ammonia and hydrogen, which introduce new safety considerations Paul Herbert, Principal Technology Specialist at Lloyd’s Register, said: “With much of the global fleet expected to remain in service well into the next decade, retrofit projects will play a critical role in shipping’s decarbonisation journey. The challenge is no longer identifying technologies, but understanding how those technologies can be safely, practically and economically integrated into existing ships while meeting increasingly demanding regulatory requirements. The attached image shows the bow of a large cargo ship in dry dock. Image by jaslagman0 from Pixabay “As the industry evaluates a wider range of fuel and efficiency solutions, retrofit projects are becoming more complex. This guidance has been developed to give the industry a practical framework for navigating those challenges. By bringing alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies together in a single document, we are helping owners take a more informed and structured approach to retrofit decision-making and project delivery.” The Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices is available from LR’s Retrofit Research programme: Ship Retrofitting | Retrofit Research Programme | LR LR’s Retrofit Research programme serves as a comprehensive hub for ship retrofitting insights, providing annual reports, publications and tools that monitor retrofitting demand, capabilities, and adoption trends. Source: Lloyd’s Register 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
