articles.body: ENGINE: Americas Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 North America Bunker demand has been strong in Houston on the US Gulf Coast, and prompt availability of all three grades is tight. A few suppliers have run out of HSFO and VLSFO and are thus unable to offer stems. Other suppliers recommend lead times of 6-8 days for both grades, a trader said. LSMGO can be supplied with lead times of 4-5 days. Rough weather has delayed bunker operations at the Galveston Offshore Lightering Area (GOLA) over the past week. High wind gusts and rough seas could disrupt operations at the anchorage from 16-18 October. Wind gusts could reach 42 knots on Friday night and early Saturday, with waves of up to 2.4 metres forecast on Saturday. This is expected to delay bunker deliveries further, a trader said. Deliveries are currently made on a first-come, first-served basis, subject to weather. Sea fog could also slow bunker deliveries in the US Gulf early on Friday. The risk of fog off Galveston is high from midnight until midday on Friday, with visibility forecast to drop to two nautical miles in the early hours. In New Orleans, strong wind gusts could disrupt bunker operations from late on 16 October until 18 October, with gusts of up to 31 knots forecast early on Saturday, a source said. On the East Coast, demand in New York is steady. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is okay, with most suppliers recommending lead times of 5-7 days. HSFO is slightly tighter and needs at least a week’s notice, a source tells ENGINE. Strong wind gusts could disrupt bunker deliveries in New York from 16-17 October, with wind gusts of up to 27 knots forecast on Saturday. Suppliers may need to keep a tug on standby to support bunker barges in the high winds, a trader said. In Los Angeles and Long Beach, the bunker market has been steady and good weather at both ports has been conducive for bunker operations. LSMGO availability is okay, with lead times of 4-5 days. VLSFO and HSFO availability is tight and is expected to tighten further. Lead times currently stretch to a week, a source said. In Vancouver, Canada, availability of all three conventional grades is good. HSFO and LSMGO have typically been delivered within 4-5 days over the past week. VLSFO is also available and needs at least five days of lead time, a trader said. Latin America and the Caribbean The bunker market in Panama is strong, and no weather disruptions are expected at Balboa and Cristobal. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is normal at both the ports, with recommended lead times of 3-6 days. HSFO needs slightly longer, with typical lead times of 4-7 days, a source said. No weather disruptions are expected at Freeport in the Bahamas, St. Eustatius or off Trinidad, with wind gusts below 20 knots forecast through Saturday. Cruise ships take priority for bunker deliveries at Freeport and St. Eustatius, where vessels are supplied at anchorage. Off Trinidad, deliveries are made while vessels are underway. In Colombia, availability of all three conventional grades is normal in Cartagena, Santa Marta and Barranquilla, with recommended lead times of 5-8 days, a source said. VLSFO availability is okay in Callao, with recommended lead times of 5-8 days. LSMGO is tight at the port, with lead times of over a week, and HSFO is tight and available only under prior consultation, a source said. VLSFO and MGO avails are okay across Chilean ports, with recommended lead times of 5-8 days. HSFO is not available in Chile. In Brazil, VLSFO and LSMGO availability are tight in Rio de Janeiro and both grades are available only under prior consultation, a trader said. HSFO is also available at the port under prior consultation. VLSFO and LSMGO availability at Santos is normal, with recommended lead times of 5-8 days. The earliest delivery date for VLSFO and LSMGO in Paranagua is 18 October, and supply is tight after that. In Rio Grande, the earliest delivery date for both grades is 20 October. In Argentina’s Zona Comun, VLSFO and LSMGO are tight and available only under prior consultation, a source said. Deliveries are made on a first-come, first-served basis, subject to weather. No weather disruptions are expected at the port this week, with gusts of up to 18 knots forecast on Friday. articles.body: GTMaritime looks beyond email with GT Connect, bringing a new approach to maritime collaboration in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 GTMaritime has launched GT Connect, a new maritime collaboration platform that connects vessel and shore-based teams, their communications and the operational work that follows. Building on GTMaritime’s experience in maritime communications, GT Connect brings conversations, people, information and tasks together within a shared operational workspace, helping teams work more efficiently, maintain visibility and make better-informed decisions. Email remains fundamental to maritime operations, but the work generated by those communications often continues beyond the email itself. A conversation may lead to a task, a booking, a technical case, a document that needs reviewing or an action that has to be followed through by another member of the team. In practice, the resulting information can become fragmented across individual inboxes, spreadsheets, messaging platforms, software systems and people’s own knowledge of what has happened. Jamie Jones, Managing Director, GTMaritime GT Connect has been developed to address that gap. Rather than replacing email, the platform connects communications with the operational activity surrounding them. Conversations can sit alongside vessels, users, tasks, cases, bookings, documents and configured workflows within a shared operational workspace. The objective is to make it easier for operational maritime teams to understand not simply what has been communicated, but what is happening as a result, what needs to happen next and who is responsible for it. Jamie Jones, Managing Director of GTMaritime, says the distinction is important because maritime businesses already generate large volumes of operational information. The challenge is often maintaining the context around that information as work moves between individuals, departments, vessels and shore teams. For example, a communication may concern an engineer due to attend a vessel during its next port call. Within GT Connect, that conversation can be associated with the vessel and the relevant operational process, allowing the resulting work and supporting information to remain connected as the activity progresses. This also has implications for continuity. Responsibilities in shipping frequently move between people and teams. Crews rotate, people join and leave vessels, and shoreside responsibilities can move between individuals. Information held solely within a personal inbox can therefore become difficult for the next person to recover or understand. GT Connect helps preserve that organisational context, keeping conversations, decisions and operational activity accessible as responsibilities change. Communications remain available and searchable, while changes to cases, workflows and other controlled activity can be traced through their histories and audit records. Secure operational chat across shore and vessel teams GT Connect also provides real-time operational chat for direct conversations, private groups and workstreams. Shore teams can communicate with colleagues, teams and current vessel-role holders, while access follows workspace permissions and active team or vessel assignments. Chat messages and attachments remain internal to the workspace, and relevant exchanges can be linked to conversations, cases, tasks and bookings so that decisions retain their operational context. Putting AI to work with operational context AI adds another layer of intelligence to GT Connect, helping maritime teams make better use of the information already available to them. By drawing on relevant conversations, vessel information and operational context, AI can help users quickly interpret communications, identify key information and understand what needs attention. Rather than simply summarising messages, it provides practical assistance within everyday workflows, helping teams save time, reduce manual effort and make more informed decisions. Developed around maritime workflows GT Connect has been shaped through close collaboration with maritime industry stakeholders, combining GTMaritime’s experience in ship-shore communications with input from people managing day-to-day maritime operations. This collaborative approach has helped ensure the platform addresses real operational challenges, from managing shared communications and maintaining continuity between crews to improving visibility of responsibilities and outstanding work. Rather than asking shipping companies to adapt to another generic collaboration tool, GT Connect has been developed around the way maritime teams actually work. Feedback has particularly focused on vessel communications, shared mailboxes, handovers, ownership of work and the transition from a communication into a defined operational action. By maintaining the connection between communications and the operational work they generate, GT Connect helps maritime teams spend less time searching for information, reconstructing previous decisions and establishing who is responsible for the next action. For organisations managing large fleets and complex operations, this creates opportunities to improve efficiency, accountability and collaboration across teams. GT Connect offers a new approach to how maritime teams manage communication and collaboration. By bringing people, conversations and operational activity together around a shared understanding of what’s happening across the fleet, the platform creates opportunities for more efficient working, stronger collaboration and better-informed decisions. For GTMaritime, it’s about taking maritime communications beyond the exchange of information and making that information more valuable to the people and operations that depend on it. articles.body: Iron Ore: Australian majors diverge as Vale faces growing guidance risks in Commodity News , Dry Bulk Market 16/10/2026 September quarter performance is expected to diverge sharply across major iron ore miners. Rio Tinto’s Pilbara shipments rose y/y despite CMRG tensions, leaving annual guidance achievable, while BHP delivered a record fiscal first quarter as Jimblebar Fines fully recovered. By contrast, FMG’s CMRG dispute drove a 7% y/y shipment decline, although diversification partly cushioned the loss. Vale faces growing guidance risk after exports from Brazil fell 7% y/y. Executive summary The Iron Ore Miners Quarterly report, part of Kpler’s Iron Ore and Steel Insight offering, was previously published as Market Pulse as of August 2026. The report provides forecasts of iron ore producers’ quarterly output and shipments ahead of their official results, using proprietary modelling that combines Kpler’s vessel-tracking and trade-flow data with analysts’ market expertise. • Australian iron ore majors generally outperformed their Atlantic peers in Q3. Rio Tinto’s physical flows remained resilient despite CMRG restrictions, while BHP posted record September-quarter exports. FMG was the exception, with its dispute with CMRG sharply reducing Chinese sales. • In the Atlantic, Vale’s exports contracted y/y as elevated freight costs, softer Chinese steel demand, and greater competition squeezed volumes, raising the prospect of a guidance cut. • Rio-owned IOC, included in our forecast for the first time, staged a sizeable quarterly recovery, but its multi-year operational reset and persistent logistics disruptions mean full-year guidance remains at risk. Rio Tinto: CMRG tensions have yet to materially affect overall Pilbara shipments Rio Tinto exported 83.90Mt of iron ore from Western Australia in Q3 2026, up 2% y/y, despite souring relations with China Mineral Resources Group (CMRG). CMRG reportedly asked some Chinese steelmakers to suspend negotiations with Rio Tinto in early August and then asked them to hold off purchases of Pilbara Blend in early September. So far, however, the impact on overall physical Pilbara flows remains limited, even though some of the volumes may translate only into Rio’s portside inventory in China rather than into actual sales, and shipments of Pilbara blend fines are starting to slow down. China still accounted for 81.50% of Rio’s Q3 exports from Western Australia, broadly unchanged from a year earlier, suggesting that the miner has made little effort to diversify its customer base. We expect Rio Tinto to officially report 86.20Mt of Pilbara iron ore sales (100% basis) in Q3, up 2.20% y/y, when it publishes its operational results on 13 October. Combined with reported H1 sales of 157.65Mt, this would lift nine-month volumes to approximately 243.85Mt, leaving 79.15–94.15Mt required in Q4 to meet full-year guidance of 323–338Mt. Rio’s Q4 sales have averaged 86.93Mt over the past five years, suggesting that the midpoint of guidance remains achievable at a normal seasonal shipment pace. CMRG nevertheless remains the principal downside risk. Any escalation could begin to affect physical sales after having so far been largely confined to commercial negotiations. Key indicators to watch include any update on CMRG discussions in Rio’s Q3 operational review, Chinese port inventories of Pilbara Blend and any visits to China by senior Rio executives. At Simandou, total exports surged 66% q/q to 8.74Mt in Q3, although we estimate that BWCS continued to account for most shipments. SimFer volumes should increase further in Q4 as permanent crushing facilities come online and locomotive availability ceases to be a major logistical bottleneck. Rio Tinto-owned IOC: Q3 recovery insufficient to remove guidance risk Iron Ore Company of Canada (IOC), Rio Tinto’s majority-owned Canadian operation, exported 5.03Mt in Q3 2026, recovering from 3.30Mt in Q1 and 3.77Mt in Q2. The improvement appears to reflect a recovery in port unloading capacity and improved pellet machine availability. Nevertheless, Q3 exports remained 6.40% below the year-ago level. IOC’s strategic operational reset, launched in late 2025, is designed to catch up on deferred waste stripping, improve long-term pit health and restore operational flexibility. Rio has indicated that this process will take several years, during which concentrate production is expected to remain constrained. Logistics has added another layer of disruption, with the QNS&L Railway suffering at least four outages this year due to wildfires, a derailment and adverse weather. We expect Rio Tinto to report 3.70–4.20Mt of IOC sales (100% basis) in Q3, bringing nine-month sales to 10.16–10.66Mt. IOC would therefore need to sell at least 4.34Mt in Q4 merely to reach the bottom of its 15–18Mt full-year guidance. That target remains possible, but increasingly demanding. IOC’s Q4 sales have averaged 4.15Mt over the past five years, while concentrate production remains constrained by the operational reset. High shipping costs have cut margins on cargoes to East Asian destinations. A reduction to full-year guidance, therefore, remains a material risk when Rio Tinto reports its Q3 operational results. Vale: Q3 weakness raises the prospect of a full-year guidance cut Vale exported 77.30Mt of iron ore from Brazil in Q3 2026, down 7.30% y/y, the sharpest annual contraction since 2020. Shipments to the miner’s major markets, including East Asia, Southeast Asia and Europe, all declined y/y. India was the main exception: although still a relatively small market for Vale, shipments to the country reached a record 3.20Mt, supported by capacity expansion among customers such as JSW Steel. The Q3 export decline reflects a combination of demand, freight and competitive pressures: • Chinese crude steel production is expected to fall around 4% y/y in Q3, while preliminary data indicate that the growth of quarterly iron ore imports was at the second lowest since 2022. • Freight became considerably more expensive, with the C3 Tubarão–Qingdao rate averaging $36.79/t, up 57% y/y. Although Vale said during its Q2 results that spot freight exposure had been reduced to below 10% for H2, the commercial impact appears greater than the headline exposure would imply. • Competition has also intensified. High freight rates have strengthened the relative advantage of Australian ore in Asian markets, while accelerating Simandou exports are adding another source of higher-grade supply into China. • Other headwinds may include lower third-party purchases from smaller Brazilian miners, a demanding Q3 2025 comparison base, delays to the recovery of the Fábrica and Viga mines, and a gradual rather than rapid ramp-up of Vale’s Oman pellet operations following their partial restart in late June. We now expect Vale to officially report around 88.80Mt of iron ore production (including third-party purchases) in Q3, down 5.70% y/y from 94.40Mt and substantially below our previous forecast of 94.50Mt. Combined with 153.93Mt in H1, nine-month production would reach roughly 243Mt, leaving 92–102Mt required in Q4 to achieve the existing full-year guidance of 335–345Mt. Given current market conditions, production above 92Mt in the final quarter appears challenging. With softer Chinese demand, high freight costs and broader pressure on Brazilian producers persisting, the possibility that Vale will follow CSN in lowering its full-year production guidance when it reports Q3 results remains on the table. BHP: Jimblebar Fines stage a full recovery BHP exported 74.30Mt of iron ore from Western Australia in the September quarter, up 5.50% y/y and the highest fiscal first-quarter volume on record. A series of industrial actions involving port and maintenance workers in July and August ultimately had little impact on quarterly shipments, highlighting BHP’s ability to mitigate disruptions through contingency staffing, scheduling and catch-up loadings. The standout development was the recovery in Jimblebar Fines. Shipments surged 28% y/y to a record 15Mt, compared with 8.10Mt in the June quarter and just 2.16Mt in the March quarter. Around 14Mt was shipped to China, also a record, indicating that Chinese demand for the grade has fully recovered following the restrictions imposed between September 2025 and early 2026. At the same time, shipments to non-Chinese customers, particularly Vietnam, continued to increase. We expect BHP to report 73.90Mt of WAIO production (100% basis) in its operational review on 20 October. This would represent the strongest September-quarter production performance in the company’s history and a solid start to FY2027, for which BHP has set guidance of 286–298Mt. Industrial relations remain the main near-term operational risk. Further short-duration strikes at Port Hedland remain possible, with the Fair Work Commission’s bargaining proceedings potentially extending through December. However, recent experience suggests that the ultimate impact on quarterly shipments may remain manageable. FMG: CMRG dispute drives sharp September-quarter contraction FMG exported 45.20Mt of iron ore from Western Australia in the September quarter, down 7.30% y/y, with the decline largely attributable to restrictions associated with its dispute with CMRG. Shipments to China fell to a two-year low of 39.20Mt. FMG has responded by accelerating diversification. Exports to non-Chinese markets surged 36.70% y/y to a record 5.93Mt, supported particularly by stronger sales into Southeast Asia and India. However, these gains were insufficient to compensate for weaker Chinese demand. We now expect FMG to officially report Q1 FY2027 shipments of 46.20Mt (100% basis), down from 47.70Mt previously. This would represent a 7.40% y/y decline and leave 151–161Mt to be shipped over the remaining three quarters to achieve full-year guidance of 197–207Mt. Despite the weak start, we see little likelihood that FMG will lower its annual guidance in its Q1 FY2027 results, to be announced on 22 October. A partial or interim agreement with CMRG remains possible during the December quarter, even if a comprehensive long-term agreement proves more difficult. Continued growth in sales to Southeast Asia and India should also provide a partial offset, although these markets remain too small to fully replace China. Source: Kpler 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: The Hellenic Institute of Marine Technology (H.I.M.T.) successfully organised the 20th Annual Marine Technology Conference, held on 6 and 7 October 2026 at the Eugenides Foundation, preceded by a pre-conference event on 5 October at the V.Ships Auditorium in Piraeus. This year’s conference was of particular significance, marking the twentieth anniversary of an established institution that has become a reference point for scientific knowledge, technological innovation and collaboration across the maritime sector. With more than 900 registrations, the Conference brought together representatives from the shipping industry, academic & research institutions, public bodies and businesses, confirming the strong interest in the technological developments shaping the future of shipping. The Conference was officially opened by Mr. George Pratikakis, President of H.I.M.T., who highlighted the significance of the anniversary and the Conference’s longstanding contribution to scientific dialogue and the exchange of expertise. He emphasized that the Institute, founded in 1972, continues to operate as an independent scientific organization, bridging research, academic knowledge and the shipping industry. Emphasis was placed on the challenges of the energy transition, digitalization, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity, with innovation and investment in human capital identified as essential prerequisites for the competitiveness of Greek shipping. Opening addresses were delivered by Mr. George Alexandratos, President of the Hellenic Chamber of Shipping; Mr. Charalampos Simantonis, President of the Hellenic Shortsea Ship-owners Association and the European Shortsea Network; Mr. Vassilis Korkidis, President of the Piraeus Chamber of Commerce and Industry; Mr. Dionysios Theodoratos, President of the Association of Passenger Shipping Companies; Dr Matthew Maheras, President of A.M.M.I.T.E.C.; Dr Ioannis Chatzigeorgiou, Rector of the National Technical University of Athens; Dr Dimosthenis Kyriazis, Rector of the University of Piraeus; Dr George Galanis, Dean of the Hellenic Naval Academy; and Dr Thomas Mazarakos, President of the Department of Naval Architecture at the University of West Attica. The pre-conference event on 5 October, entitled “Research and Education in the Service of Innovation”, focused on connecting research and education with the needs of the shipping industry. The first panel explored the role of Industrial PhD programmes in fostering collaboration between universities and businesses, while the second addressed the technological transformation of Merchant Marine Academies and the evolving requirements for education and professional training. The discussions brought together representatives from universities, government, shipping companies and educational institutions. The two main days of the Conference featured scientific papers and presentations of advanced technological applications, covering a broad range of marine technology topics, including energy efficiency and alternative fuels, emissions reduction, propulsion systems, digitalization, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, ship and equipment safety, and developments in the shipbuilding industry. The Conference also provided companies with an opportunity to showcase their solutions and innovations, fostering networking and collaboration among participants. Two major panel discussions addressed the challenges and prospects of modern shipping. The first, entitled “Powering Shipping Through Uncertainty: Alternative Fuels, Safety Challenges and Geopolitical Realities”, examined the challenges associated with the transition to alternative fuels, safety considerations and geopolitical developments. The second, entitled “Profitable Waters Ahead? Navigating Market Volatility in a Changing Maritime Economy”, focused on fluctuations in the shipping market and the prospects for sustainable growth and profitability in an increasingly dynamic economic environment. The Conference proceedings culminated in a roundtable discussion entitled “Ships Are Changing Faster Than People: Building the Maritime Workforce of the Future”, moderated by Dr Nikolaos Liapis, Director of H.I.M.T. The discussion featured Mr. Miltiadis Varvitsiotis, former Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy and CEO of Skaramangas Shipyards; Mr. Charalampos Simantonis, President of the Hellenic Shortsea Ship-owners Association and the European Shortsea Network; Ms. Danai Bezantakou, President of the International Propeller Club, Port of Piraeus, and CEO of Navigator Shipping Consultants Ltd.; and Ms. Elena Athoussaki, Chief Sustainability Officer of Motor Oil Group and Principal Organizer of the ESG Shipping Awards. The discussion highlighted the need for the maritime workforce to adapt to rapid technological and operational changes, as well as the importance of developing new skills to meet the demands of the shipping industry of the future. The Conference concluded on the evening of 7 October with the official Conference Dinner, held at 20:00 at the Piraeus Marine Club. During the event, α plaque of honor was given to the late Mr. George Vozikis. Through his longstanding commitment and continuous contribution, Mr. Vozikis played a significant role in the work and development of H.I.M.T., forming part of the collective effort that has consistently supported the Institute’s mission. The 20th Annual Marine Technology Conference reaffirmed H.I.M.T.’s vital role in advancing scientific knowledge, technological innovation and collaboration between the shipping industry and the research community. Reaching this twentieth-anniversary milestone represents both a significant achievement and a starting point for new initiatives aimed at strengthening the international outlook and global presence of Greek marine technology. The Institute extends its sincere thanks to all participants, speakers, authors of scientific papers, sponsors and supporters who contributed to the success of the Conference.

articles.title: The Markets Impacting the Revival of US Naval & Commercial Shipbuilding
articles.summary: The U.S. Maritime Industry is sifting through a nearly two-year decision process after Executive Order 14269 announcements of “Maritime Dominance” of April 9th 2025. Initially reported as the strongest federal support in decades, longer periods…
articles.body: The Markets Impacting the Revival of US Naval & Commercial Shipbuilding Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Robert Kunkel , Contributor Robert Kunkel, President of Alternative Marine Technologies... October 15, 2026 Copyright IanDewarPhotography/AdobeStock The U.S. Maritime Industry is sifting through a nearly two-year decision process after Executive Order 14269 announcements of “Maritime Dominance” of April 9th 2025. Initially reported as the strongest federal support in decades, longer periods of delays have also occurred as congress debates the Ships for America Act which has been passed from committee to committee in Congress. Legislation proposed to support American shipbuilding and the US flag commercial fleet and to date, has not reached the floor. Recently, the Maritime Administration advised the government effort is a different maritime revival. An understatement considering the Federal government’s first move was to issue a “Jones Act” waiver on March 17, 2026, allowing foreign vessels to trade in the coastal energy market. To be fair, the announcement was made through the Department of Homeland Security and reported without MarAd’s knowledge. The waiver disrupted U.S. flag coastal energy trading on all three coasts and has raised many unanswered questions on the direction the Administration is taking or for that matter who is making the decisions. The irony of the revival statement is the fact that the “Act” has long been described as the backbone of the country’s maritime industry. Considering the current global geopolitical events, the waiver decisions also question the claim of National Security, historically supported by Transcom and Military Sealift Command. Most would agree it could not be more important at this time. With issues continuing in the Straits of Hormuz, the waiver’s promise of gasoline price reduction did not occur during the first five months of foreign vessel trading. The energy costs continue to rise despite an extension put into place on August 13, 2026. Attempts to track the foreign flag cargo movements have been poor at best with estimates ranging from 200 to 400 voyages occurring during the two periods. Considering MarAd’s understanding that cargo is a part of this revival, it would be our opinion coastal movements is an important market that should be considered as a US “Maritime Dominance” priority. Certainly, with the fact that we have now invested over one and a half billion dollars in state maritime training vessels to recover the lack of seafaring labor. It is not only cargo; the success of a “market” is what drives commercial shipbuilding and investment. Simply put, the direction and success of commercial US shipbuilding is not only preference cargo. It is building at competitive costs to enter a market that employs American seafarers and provide the ability to renew an aging fleet. The lack of US shipyard subsidy is the problem and it is needed to meet that goal. We cannot compete commercially against foreign operating costs and capital of ship construction or labor. The original Ships For America Act legislation contains a shipbuilding incentives subsection 53801 interpreted to believe Congress and the Federal Government understands shipyard subsidy is required for commercial shipbuilding if we are to make any attempt to compete with any foreign shipyard. The description of the incentive allows a comparison of a US build cost to a foreign build of a coastal registered vessel not competing with current operators or looking to trade in an area where the specific vessel type is not available. The approval results in subsidy against the comparable US to foreign cost differential. Amtech has submitted a project to the Maritime Administrator with that objective. A US shipyard partner and a financial supporter are involved who have built the vessel type in foreign yards and a US yard to confirm the costs. Here is the problem. The foreign contracted cost is not a real number. The delivered foreign contract takes into account the shipbuilding subsidies provided by their governments whether Chinese, Korean, Japanese or European (the ship design has been built in more than several foreign countries). The US shipyard costs do not. In our opinion the project may open doors to understanding the US “cost to build” problem when competing against foreign yards. Our intent is to continue to support the industry as we have for decades. That said if the current administration is looking to reinvent the wheel, look to those who were around when the wheel was actually built. Many of the industry problems are repeated historical events which have not been corrected and if not addressed now will result in the revival failing again without accomplishing simple goals. An undated still image released on Oct. 6 from video taken by an Arabian Fox MAST-13 of an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy patrol speedboat in the Strait of Hormuz. Seven task forces falling under U.S. 5th Fleet integrated 12 different unmanned platforms with manned ships for “manned-unmanned teaming” operations tracking Iranian Navy and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy (IRGCN) ships and small boats over several days during routine patrols in and around the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Navy photo Begin by completely separating Naval and commercial ship construction. The successful Far East yards have been structured in this manner for decades. Owner/Operators build according to market supply and demand. Shipyards design and build according to their own markets and business models. Military and commercial ship construction are two different animals. Naval shipbuilding markets follow geopolitical events and we are drowning in those global events as we speak. Give the Department of War credit for understanding that Navy shipbuilding has changed. Drones, UAV, Autonomous surface, conventional submarines and Arctic requirements are the latest additions to our Destroyers, Nuclear Carriers and Submarines fleets. US shipbuilding defense capacity and government investment has already responded to these new problems and requirements. The US Navy was originally built to serve and protect the American coasts, our commercial ships and trade. The global shift in that operation occurred after World War II as the United States emerged as the world’s industrial and naval superpower. The only fleet left standing The 1944 Bretton Woods agreement established a postwar international financial system and the U.S. committed to a strategy guaranteeing a secure, free use of the oceans for all nations, including former adversaries. This created the maritime environment necessary for modern globalization. We were no longer tasked to defend or project power. The US Navy protected free trade. Free trade is now under attack. Circa 1979 the U.S. reestablished the post-WWII role by establishing the DoD Freedom of Navigation Program. The Navy regularly conducted freedom of navigation operations worldwide to challenge and ensure international sea lanes remained open under international law. As many debate the lack of Naval budget and government support during the post-cold war period, take a moment to realize what the actual threat was to commercial shipping and the US flag vessels that were operating internationally. We are being challenged to return to that role with the continued threat of a “ghost” fleet and free trade is again being defended with force. Nearly 10 years later, Operation Earnest Will (1987–1988) was developed during the tanker war of the Iran-Iraq conflict. Iranian forces utilized mines and speedboats to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. In response to the escalation, threatening over 20% of the world's oil supply, the U.S. Navy launched its largest convoy escort operation since WWII. We reflagged Kuwaiti oil tankers and actively escorted tonnage through the Gulf, while destroying Iranian gunboats and mining platforms to keep the Strait open. Apologies for not wanting to miss this opportunity to quote Yogi Berra as we compare the current Middle East situation as an example of history repeating itself. Its “Déjà vu all over again” We previously noted the dates the Executive orders and commerce reports were issued. The Straits were open and oil flowed. The Naval ship construction concerns at that time prepared for an Indo Pacific theater requiring both projecting military power and defending both ally and homeland. The latest Middle East conflict has now presented two fronts on a possible war footing. Ukraine and Russia have presented a third. Through more than several Federal Administrations, strategic Pentagon reports have advised the existing Naval fleet was not capable of supporting two fronts. Naval shipbuilding needs to be funded, take precedence, and utilize our shipyard capacity to build a war time labor force and deliver a fleet capable of reestablishing free trade and preserve National Security. Add the control of Greenland to the discussions or the Canadian Prime Minister stating in a September 2026 interview with the New York Times that his government examined the possibility of a U.S. military invasion of Canada, describing it as an "extreme tail risk", and ship construction takes on a entirely different discussion. Unfortunately, US commercial shipbuilding may have to take a back seat for the moment. Extreme geopolitical events effect trade. Commercial markets adjust to those changes and with that so do technical and operational requirements of ship types. Simple examples of the new interest in Venezuelan sources of methanol, the new routes of the Arctic requiring ice class tonnage, or the rebuilding of Ukraine & Cuba will take time to develop and significant risk analysis. The new interest in developing construction with allied shipyards under the “Finland” ice breaker concept or the “bridge” concept of Naval Auxiliary support vessels with new designs and efficiencies look to decrease that time. As commercial shipbuilders we have to meet a different cost standard and deliver according to an investment business plan to compete in a foreign market or for that matter support our military. Our long-term goal this time around is to make sure Yogi is not quoted again and let a new history develop. * As published in the October 2026 edition of Marine News.

October 15, 2026 © GT Wings GT Wings has announced the latest addition to its wind-assisted propulsion product range, AirWingS, a new compact and lightweight Jet Sail developed to address the operational requirements of smaller commercial vessels. The new design expands the AirWing product line to address a broader segment of the commercial shipping market. With a streamlined lightweight configuration, the AirWingS has been developed specifically for smaller vessels where vessel size, available deck space and weight considerations can influence the suitability of wind-assisted propulsion technology. The launch is the next step in GT Wings' strategy to develop a scalable family of AirWing Jet Sails, enabling the technology to be adapted to differing requirements across the global commercial fleet. New product launch alongside first commercial production The announcement comes as GT Wings marks a milestone in the commercialization of its technology, with an Open House event showcasing the first customer-ordered AirWing units nearing completion at its partner Zunsion Technology's manufacturing facility in Nantong. GT Wings announced a strategic manufacturing partnership with Zunsion Technology in March 2026. The partnership established a framework for industrial-scale production of AirWing systems in China, combining GT Wings' wind propulsion and systems integration expertise with Zunsion's manufacturing and assembly capabilities. Open House attendees toured the facility and viewed two nearly completed 20m AirWing units ahead of delivery. The program also included a keynote address by Ms. Marie Langrishe, Trade Counsellor for Technology and Industry, UK Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Technology of the UK Embassy to China in Beijing, as well as a technical update on the latest AirWing product developments. The event brought together representatives from China, France, Hong Kong, Japan, Norway, the United Kingdom, and the wider international shipping industry, providing an opportunity to discuss the role of advanced manufacturing and maritime technology in supporting shipping's transition towards lower-carbon operations. articles.summary: C.H. Robinson has released its 2027 Freight Market Outlook, identifying five major factors that could influence transportation costs, capacity and supply chain operations over the coming year. articles.body: C.H. Robinson has released its 2027 Freight Market Outlook, identifying five major factors that could influence transportation costs, capacity and supply chain operations over the coming year. The report examines developments across ocean shipping, air freight, road transport, intermodal services and port operations. It highlights how regulatory changes, capacity pressures and geopolitical uncertainty could affect the movement of goods across global markets. According to C.H. Robinson, shippers will need to assess risks across different transport modes and prepare alternative arrangements to limit potential disruptions. Five factors influencing freight markets The outlook identifies transportation regulations as a key area to watch in 2027. Changes to safety requirements, emissions rules, customs procedures and cross-border compliance could affect operating costs and available transport capacity. Legal and liability developments are another concern. Rising insurance costs and changes in legal responsibilities could influence how logistics providers operate and price their services. The report also examines capacity growth. C.H. Robinson notes that an increase in overall transport capacity does not necessarily mean that sufficient equipment or services will be available on every trade route. Regional imbalances and demand for specialised equipment could continue to create constraints. Extreme weather is identified as a fourth factor, particularly because disruptions to ports, roads and other infrastructure can affect freight movements well beyond the areas directly impacted. Finally, geopolitical tensions remain an important source of uncertainty. Trade policies, tariffs, conflicts and changes in manufacturing locations could influence shipping routes, transport demand and supply chain costs. Shippers urged to prepare for changing conditions Rather than predicting a single direction for freight markets, C.H. Robinson’s outlook focuses on how conditions could differ between regions and transport modes. The company recommends that shippers monitor capacity and cost developments, establish contingency plans and consider alternative routes, transport modes and logistics providers. The report also highlights the importance of reviewing sourcing and procurement strategies as market conditions change. C.H. Robinson’s 2027 outlook presents these five factors as potential influences on freight markets rather than confirmed developments, reflecting the uncertainty surrounding global transportation in the year ahead.

The vessel subsequently sank, with all 21 crew members safely evacuated. The image has not been independently verified. U.S. Central Command says the United States and its regional partners control the Strait of Hormuz, citing more than 40 commercial ships moving through the waterway in the past 24 hours, even as maritime security officials warn that attacks on merchant vessels are increasing and the threat to shipping remains severe. The statement Thursday came as the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) released a new assessment documenting a series of attacks on commercial shipping, including the sinking of a containership, and warning that further strikes remain highly likely. “The United States and regional partners control the strait as commercial vessels continue to transit despite unwarranted IRGC aggression,” CENTCOM said in a statement rejecting three Iranian claims . But the military’s assertion of control comes against a markedly different picture of commercial shipping conditions. Traffic remains far below prewar levels, vessels continue to face attacks along established transit routes, and Iran is still attempting to influence how ships move through the strait. According to JMIC’s October 15 advisory , U.S.-facilitated traffic totaled 121 vessel transits between October 11 and 14, an average of approximately 30 ships per day. That compares with a historical average of roughly 138 daily transits in 2025, before the war. CENTCOM’s latest figure of more than 40 ships covers a different 24-hour period and may indicate an increase in traffic. Still, the four-day JMIC average represents only about 22% of the prewar benchmark. Independent commercial tracking continues to show substantially fewer transits than U.S. military-assisted figures. JMIC reported single-digit daily movements in its separate tracking data, although the two sources use different methodologies and do not measure the same categories of traffic. The distinction matters because while ships are continuing to pass through Hormuz, the volume of traffic remains a fraction of normal levels. JMIC maintained its threat assessment for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE , warning that deliberate hostile action against commercial vessels remains highly likely. The latest advisory documented eight projectile attacks in the strait on October 11 and 13, involving four tankers and four containerships. A separate attack on the products tanker PETRO DOLPHIN near Sohar, Oman, left two crew members missing. The most serious recent incident involved the Singapore-flagged GFS PRIDE , which was struck by a projectile on October 13 , caught fire and subsequently sank on October 14. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. CENTCOM rejected an Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claim that the vessel had struck a naval mine while traveling along an unauthorized route. “The civilian container ship M/V GFS Pride was hit by an IRGC projectile,” CENTCOM said, adding that the vessel sank while being towed to shore. The military also maintained that the strait’s primary shipping routes remain clear of mines. JMIC separately said there was no evidence supporting Iran’s claim that a mine caused the sinking. However, the advisory continued to warn mariners about potential mining activity within and around the established traffic separation scheme. It also warned of a continuing threat from IRGC surveillance, drone overflights, radio hailing and attempts to direct merchant ships toward the northern Iranian-controlled route. Vessels using the southern Omani corridor remain exposed to attacks, while those broadcasting their positions through the Automatic Identification System (AIS) face an elevated targeting risk, according to JMIC. The organization also cautioned mariners about floating containers and debris near the wreck of GFS PRIDE . The latest attacks are part of a broader escalation that began before October. JMIC now counts 149 confirmed vessel incidents across the region since March 1, including nine newly documented incidents in its latest reporting period. The International Maritime Organization separately lists 113 highlighted confirmed incidents and 24 seafarer fatalities as of October 14. The two organizations maintain different incident datasets and their totals are not directly comparable. Meanwhile, large numbers of commercial vessels remain at anchor throughout the region. JMIC reported approximately 180 vessels near Fujairah and Khor Fakkan, another 178 between Dubai, Jebel Ali and Ras Al Khaimah, and 74 around Musandam and Sohar as of October 15. The security situation is further complicated by the continuing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports. According to the latest figures cited by JMIC, U.S. forces had redirected 135 commercial vessels and disabled four during blockade enforcement operations as of October 10-11. Neutral shipping remains permitted to transit, although vessels can expect military hailing, monitoring and possible inspections. The latest JMIC advisory also warned that ships using either the northern Iranian-controlled route or the southern Omani corridor should expect continued security risks and reduced traffic. That leaves a significant gap between the military’s claim of control and the conditions facing commercial operators. U.S. forces are facilitating vessel movements through the strait, and commercial ships continue to transit. But attacks have continued despite the military presence, and shipping volumes remain well below their prewar levels. For shipowners, charterers and crews, the remaining question is whether the United States can provide enough security for normal commercial operations to resume, rather than simply keeping the waterway open to traffic willing to accept the risks. articles.title: Seven Sailors Missing After Chemical Tankers Struck Near Romania
articles.summary: Rescuers searched on Thursday for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine.Romanian President…
articles.body: Seven Sailors Missing After Chemical Tankers Struck Near Romania Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 15, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zerophoto Rescuers searched on Thursday for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones but declined to say whether Russia was responsible, while a NATO military source said the drones came from Russia. "The drones that caused the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin," the NATO source said. The two vessels were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina canal leading into the Danube River, a major export route used by Ukraine as Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukraine's Black Sea ports. One was inside Romanian territorial waters and the other just outside. The missing crew were among 12 sailors aboard the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader, which was hit 13 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, one mile outside Romanian waters. Five crew members were rescued, Romanian officials said. The second vessel, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J, caught fire after being struck 8-10 miles southeast of Sulina inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday. All crew were safe. The attacks are the latest in a series of strikes on commercial shipping in the western Black Sea. At least five other cargo vessels have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring NATO member Bulgaria over the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors reported missing or dead. Those attacks occurred outside NATO territorial waters. "The situation in the Black Sea is serious," Romania's Dan said. "Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured, and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake." SEARCH FOR MISSING SAILORS The interior ministry said it had sent two Black Hawk helicopters to the search and rescue mission, as well as two ships with medical staff on board. "At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves," it said in a statement. NATO said in a statement it was in contact with Romanian officials. It added two other vessels had been targeted in the Black Sea overnight, Marshall Islands-flagged bulk carrier Sea Destiny inside Romanian waters and Tanzanian-flagged tanker Dania J, moored in the Ukrainian Danube port of Izmail. It did not mention casualties. "NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed," NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said after meeting Dan and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Thursday. ATTACKS ON BLACK SEA SHIPPING Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since the start of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The escalating attacks on Black Sea shipping have heightened concerns over grain exports from the region. Russian attacks on Ukraine's own Black Sea ports have forced Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. Ukraine, for its part, has targeted Russian vessels near the mouth of the Don River in the Azov Sea. Bulgaria's Radev said EU leaders would discuss a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea. "We're looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu told a security conference in Warsaw earlier this week. "It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence." articles.summary: The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen.

REUTERS/Khaled Abdullah DUBAI, Oct 15 (Reuters) – The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen. By targeting infrastructure and disrupting investment events central to Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions, they aim to pressure Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to both meet Houthi demands in Yemen and persuade US President Donald Trump to ease the US blockade choking Iran’s economy, according to Saudi, Iranian and regional sources. The campaign reflects a calculation by Iran and the Houthis that Saudi Arabia’s prosperity, investment ambitions and exposure to disruption make it a vulnerable pressure point in a confrontation stretching from the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf to Bab el-Mandeb in the Red Sea. Iran, under mounting economic and military pressure following the war launched by the US and Israel on February 28, is seeking to raise the cost of Washington’s strategy by targeting its regional partners, said Michael Knights of strategic advisory Horizon Engage. “The Iranians are in a chokehold,” he said. Unable to force Washington to change course directly, Tehran and the Houthis are “hammering Saudi Arabia, they’re hammering the weak point,” he added, exploiting the kingdom’s economic vulnerability and desire for stability. The Houthis have a direct interest in easing the US blockade on Iran, their principal regional backer. A relaxation of pressure on Tehran would likely strengthen its ability to sustain the political, financial and military support and flow of weapons and cash on which the US says the movement depends. But the Houthis also have their own demands, said two Saudi sources and three regional sources familiar with Saudi thinking: an end to Saudi military operations and restrictions on Yemeni ports and airports, regular flights to Iran, restored salary payments, war compensation and an end to Riyadh’s support for Yemen’s recognized government. Their terms would consolidate Houthi rule over much of Yemen. A senior Iranian official said the Houthi attacks were part of a broader strategy by Iran and its allies to reshape the regional balance of power by targeting energy infrastructure and key shipping routes. He said Riyadh could not rely on US protection and must instead pursue negotiations, adding that Houthi attacks would continue unless Saudi restrictions were lifted. The strategy, however, leaves MbS facing a dilemma, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking say. Escalation risks a wider war that could undermine his transformation agenda, but concessions risk strengthening a movement that has challenged Saudi power for years. And the longer the conflict drags on, the greater the threat to Saudi security, investor confidence and Vision 2030. The Saudi government media office, Iran’s foreign ministry and a Houthi spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam denied that the group was acting at Iran’s behest, saying its demands were centered on longstanding humanitarian issues relating to Saudi Arabia, and included lifting restrictions on Yemeni ports, airports, easing economic restrictions, and paying civil servants’ salaries from Yemen’s own resources. “Our humanitarian demands have nothing to do with Iran or anyone else,” he said. FLAGSHIP CONFERENCES DISRUPTED Saudi Arabia has faced a widening wave of Houthi attacks over the past week, including deadly strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and a strike on Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil exporter and a backbone of the economy, which sparked a fire that spread across several floors. The attacks have disrupted Riyadh’s flagship oil conference, prompting top oil executives to withdraw, and forced organizers to offer remote participation at the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual global investment forum. The Houthis have a record of striking deep inside the kingdom, including in 2019, when attacks on Aramco facilities temporarily disrupted about 5% of global oil supply. That was after Riyadh intervened in Yemen in 2015 following the Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate before a 2022 ceasefire. However, Saudi leaders now see military pressure as their only viable option, said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center. “They reached a point of NO negotiations,” he said. “They have no other choice except military action.” The Houthis increasingly see themselves as negotiating from strength, seeking recognition of their authority in Sanaa and an easing of restrictions on Yemen, said Fawaz Gerges, a Middle East analyst at the London School of Economics. “What the Houthis are asking now is a victor’s peace,” he said. The United States has shown little appetite for another sustained campaign against the Houthis since bombing them last year over attacks on shipping in the Red Sea then agreeing a ceasefire, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking said. Washington’s reluctance leaves Riyadh facing a conflict in which military pressure alone may not deliver a decisive outcome. SAUDIS HAVE MORE TO LOSE At the start of the Houthi campaign, MbS asked Trump for help to fight the Houthis, but Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing. Trump later said he was considering possible action against the Houthis, while appearing to defer any response until after the US midterm elections. The US State Department referred to previous remarks by Trump and by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. With drones and missiles exposing vulnerabilities in Saudi defenses, analysts warn the conflict risks becoming a war of attrition in which the Houthis believe time and geography favor them. Former US negotiator Aaron David Miller said the group’s advantage lies not only in its position near the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint but also in the asymmetry of what is at stake. “Saudi infrastructure is much more valuable than Houthi infrastructure,” he said. “They have so much less to lose than the Saudis.” Yemen analyst Farea al-Muslimi said the Houthis’ campaign against Riyadh is a bid to assert regional primacy, risking a far broader conflict across the Arabian Peninsula. At the heart of the crisis, he says, is the unraveling of a 2023 Saudi-backed peace roadmap that offered the Houthis a path to political legitimacy and reconstruction funding. Under the roadmap, Riyadh was set to help fund public sector salaries and rebuilding. The Red Sea conflict has derailed that process as the Houthis deepen their alignment with Iran. “We’re heading towards the worst outcome imaginable,” al-Muslimi said. “A war worse than 2015. This time it will be bloodier, and Saudi Arabia will enter it with fewer allies.” He said no successful campaign against the Houthis was possible without Gulf unity, mainly between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. “The Houthis are not a threat to Saudi Arabia alone,” he said. “They threaten the entire Gulf and the wider region. This is not simply a Saudi war. It is a Gulf war.” (Additional reporting by Parisa Hafezi in Dubai, Ahmed Tolba in Cairo and Mohammed Ghobari; Writing by Samia Nakhoul; Editing by Aidan Lewis) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. (U.S. Navy photo) Five people have been arrested in Norway as part of an international investigation into suspected fraud and bribery involving a company providing port services to NATO warships. The arrests were carried out Wednesday, October 14, alongside coordinated searches in Romania and Germany, according to Eurojust , the European Union’s agency for criminal justice cooperation. Investigators suspect the company and its subcontractors submitted fraudulent invoices to the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) for husbandry services provided to military vessels during port calls in northwestern Europe. Husbandry services cover essential shoreside support for ships and their crews during port visits. Authorities estimate the alleged scheme has cost NATO member countries more than €1 million, although the full extent of the suspected fraud remains under investigation. The investigation also includes allegations that the company used an intermediary to bribe foreign public officials in exchange for favorable treatment in its contractual dealings with the NSPA. The NSPA, NATO’s primary logistics and procurement agency, identified the suspicious invoices and subsequently worked with investigators to provide evidence and information. Wednesday’s coordinated operation resulted in five arrests in Norway, where authorities also searched residential and business properties. In Romania, investigators searched company premises and several homes, while German authorities searched two businesses and a residence. The cross-border investigation began receiving support from Eurojust in April 2025. A joint investigation team was established three months later, bringing together authorities from Norway, Romania and the United Kingdom to share evidence and coordinate their work. German authorities also participated in the latest operation, with searches conducted in Hamburg under a European Investigation Order. Authorities involved include Norway’s economic crime agency Økokrim, Romania’s National Anticorruption Directorate, the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service and Ministry of Defence Police, and prosecutors and police in Hamburg. Eurojust did not identify the company or the individuals arrested and said it could not provide further details while the investigation continues. articles.summary: When the oil supertanker Esteem Explorer sails from the United States to Japan in late November, loaded with about 2 million barrels of crude, the journey will cost $81 million. The same journey would have cost $9.1 million last year, on average.

REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo HOUSTON/LOS ANGELES, Oct 15 (Reuters) – When the oil supertanker Esteem Explorer sails from the United States to Japan in late November, loaded with about 2 million barrels of crude, the journey will cost $81 million. The same journey would have cost $9.1 million last year, on average. The shipping cost translates into $40.50 per barrel, about nine times last year’s rate. While oil’s soaring selling price worries consumers, the Esteem Explorer’s expensive voyage illustrates how transport costs are further inflating the price. Refiners process oil into fuel to move food, retail goods and construction materials, and rising costs are stoking inflation in countries that depend on imports. Every $10-per-barrel increase in shipping costs adds about 23 cents per gallon to gasoline, said Kenneth Medlock, a fellow in energy and resource economics at the Houston-based Baker Institute for Public Policy. On that basis, the Esteem Explorer’s shipping cost works out to at least 80 cents more per gallon of gasoline than last year, according to Reuters calculations. “It’s sort of like a slow-moving train. It doesn’t all happen instantly … but the longer this drags on, the more sticky it becomes, which means you get more of a sustained impact at the grocery store, in the convenience store, at the mall,” Medlock said. “Everything gets more expensive because that’s how we move stuff around.” Freight rates account for more than 40% of the price of US oil, based on Wednesday’s price around $95 per barrel, compared with 7% on average in 2025, according to LSEG shipping and oil price data. Countries reliant on imports — including India, the Philippines and Indonesia — bear the brunt of the soaring costs, Medlock said. Record oil tanker rates are already squeezing Asian refiners’ profits, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday. Refiners process oil into gasoline for cars, diesel for semi-trucks and farm equipment, and jet fuel for airplanes. Attacks on ships related to the US-Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war have boosted freight and insurance rates. Rates to move oil from the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea in the Middle East to Asia surged to a record high around $34 per barrel this week, as shippers price in a risk premium for attacks on vessels. Fearing attack, ships are also sailing longer routes than before, tying up tankers longer. Shippers moving Saudi oil are using more vessels than before — transferring oil ship to ship — to reduce the risks for individual ships after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s main pipeline increased exports via the Strait of Hormuz. That strategy has reduced ship availability, raising costs and increasing the time cargoes are on the water. The resulting shortage of very large crude carriers such as the Esteem Explorer has lifted prices for smaller vessels. Freight rates have quadrupled since the Iran war began in February for Suezmax ships, which can carry up to 1 million barrels of oil, for a route between the US Gulf Coast and Asia, and for Aframaxes, which carry up to 750,000 barrels, on the US Gulf Coast to Europe route, according to Signal Ocean. While some shippers contract vessels for three to five years, many of them charter ships on the spot market about a month prior to loading. The long-term contracts, in which shippers and vessel owners lock in prices, could prove to be bargains for the shippers if prices rise further. Oil market upheaval has provided a windfall for tanker owners. They have recently earned as much as $1.3 million per ship per day for a round trip from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz to Asia, said Georgios Sakellariou, a Signal Ocean freight analyst. That compared with earnings of $55,000 per ship per day on average in 2025. “If you’d have told me six weeks ago that we were seeing a million dollars per day, I wouldn’t have believed you,” said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, senior analyst at maritime intelligence firm Windward. This year may be the most profitable ever, said a person at a company that owns and operates tankers primarily in the Americas. “Our expectation is that as long as there is more crude oil demand than supply, tanker rates will remain strong. However, as soon as the crude oil market loosens, tanker rates will come off the boil quickly,” said Erik Broekhuizen, head of tanker research and consulting at ship broker Poten & Partners. articles.summary: Shipowners are facing an increasingly fragmented fuel market as disruptions triggered by the Middle East conflict raise concerns about the availability and quality of supply.

Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS (Bloomberg) — Shipowners are facing an increasingly fragmented fuel market as disruptions triggered by the Middle East conflict raise concerns about the availability and quality of supply. Ships can’t always refuel at familiar ports if they’re forced on longer journeys around Africa and diverted to the Atlantic Basin to avoid escalating hostilities near the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. That’s turned other locations into so-called bunkering hubs and driven up fuel prices. “No one can treat bunkering as a routine, last-minute decision anymore,” said Frederik Guttormsen, Asia Pacific president at Stolt-Nielsen Ltd., an operator of 167 tankers that transport chemicals worldwide. “We’re securing fuel earlier and tracking availability and lead times at key ports because the risk is now as much about prompt supply as about price.” Middle East oil flows are coming under renewed strain from recent attacks in the region, including on vessels transiting Hormuz. The disruptions are pushing oil and bunker prices higher, Guttormsen said. He made the comments on the sidelines of a shipping conference in Singapore known as Sibcon. Singapore, the world’s biggest ship-refueling hub, continues to see growth, while vessels are tending to avoid Fujairah on the east coast of the United Arab Emirates, south of Hormuz. Other locations seeing higher bunkering demand since the US-Iran war include Port Louis in Mauritius, South Africa, West Africa, Brazil, Sri Lanka and Pakistan, according to participants at Sibcon. Bunkering at less familiar ports may expose shipowners to smaller or less reputable sellers, as well as wider price disparities between locations. Differences can reflect factors including fuel sourcing, access to on-spec feedstock and the availability of support services needed to ensure quality and compliance. “In this market, procurement needs to be much more structured,” said Kenneth Dam, executive director and global head of bunkering at TFG Marine, a major trader and supplier of ship fuels. Vessels are also refueling more frequently and taking smaller volumes at each stop to avoid locking in too much fuel at a particular price and port, he said. Disruptions are also becoming more frequent, leading to vessel diversions that are shifting fuel demand to other locations, said Peter Grünwaldt, head of bunkering at tanker owner Hafnia Ltd. and co-chief executive officer of bunker trader Seascale Energy. “We’re making sure we have fuel available at these ports,” he said. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Royal Navy Photo Britain has expanded its sanctions against Russia’s oil industry, targeting two more energy companies, a dozen shadow-fleet tankers and financial networks used to move money around Western restrictions. The measures, announced October 8 as part of a package of 38 sanctions targets, bring more than 90% of Russia’s oil production capacity under UK sanctions, according to the British government. The latest action also targets companies supplying equipment used in Russia’s missile and drone programs. The sanctions come as London and Washington appear to be moving in different directions on Russian oil. The Trump administration is considering easing restrictions on sanctioned tankers in an effort to reduce record-high freight rates, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Britain is urging its allies to tighten restrictions on the shipping services supporting Russia’s oil trade. At the center of the latest UK package are Russian oil companies Zarubezhneft and INK Capital. Their addition follows earlier sanctions against Russia’s largest oil producers, including Rosneft and Lukoil. British officials say the broader coverage is intended not only to restrict Russian oil revenues but also to make it harder for sanctioned producers to sell crude through companies that have not yet been blacklisted. The government’s claim that sanctions now cover more than 90% of Russian oil production capacity does not mean an equivalent share of production has stopped. Russian oil continues to reach international markets through trading and shipping networks that have adapted to Western restrictions. The package also includes 12 shadow-fleet tankers previously reported by gCaptain , bringing Britain’s total number of sanctioned shadow-fleet oil tankers to more than 600. Among the newly listed vessels is the 22-year-old product tanker Dakar , which was making a late-season voyage along Russia’s Northern Sea Route. The designation comes amid growing use of the Arctic shipping corridor by older and sanctioned vessels carrying Russian energy exports to Asian markets. Britain is also targeting the financial infrastructure behind Russia’s sanctions evasion efforts. The package includes three cryptocurrency exchanges, two payment platforms and an individual linked to financial transactions, with several targets connected to Kyrgyzstan. Two of the targeted platforms have processed transactions involving the Kremlin-backed A7 financial network, according to the UK Foreign Office. The network claimed to have moved more than $90 billion last year, an amount Britain said was equivalent to roughly half of Russia’s annual military spending. Another 17 individuals and entities were sanctioned for their involvement in supplying goods that Western governments consider important to Russia’s military production. These include importers of machine tools, electronics and other components used to manufacture ballistic missiles and drones. The UK said some suppliers have used third countries to conceal trade with Russia, highlighting the difficulty of restricting goods that can move through multiple intermediaries before reaching Russian manufacturers. The widening sanctions campaign comes at a particularly difficult time for the global tanker market. Freight rates have surged as conflict in the Middle East disrupts shipping and raises demand for available vessels. Washington is now weighing whether to allow previously sanctioned tankers to carry oil and petroleum products that are not themselves subject to U.S. sanctions. Such a move would require companies to obtain authorization from the U.S. Treasury Department, according to Reuters. The U.S. Department of Energy has said any relief would not help Russia transport its oil. However, European and British restrictions would continue to apply independently, potentially limiting the ability of those vessels to obtain insurance and other shipping services. Britain’s finance minister, John Healey, on Thursday called for tougher international restrictions on maritime services supporting Russia’s shadow fleet, underscoring the growing difference between the two countries’ approaches. The discussions follow President Donald Trump’s decision to temporarily lift restrictions on Russian diesel , another measure aimed at easing pressure on global energy markets. For shipping companies, the different approaches create an increasingly complicated sanctions environment. Even if Washington relaxes restrictions on some tankers, vessels and their commercial partners could remain subject to British and European measures. Department of War photo By Timothy Gardner and Jarrett Renshaw WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) – The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday. The discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump’s fellow Republicans in the US Senate. Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine. The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing “legal oil” to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures. The goal is to get more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was talking about easing the sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to cut record freight rates that have cut into demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group. Bits of the talk were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available. Companies seeking to use the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department to use the vessels, the official said. The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia to move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy. But Trump’s push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels. The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment. High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7. RECORD HIGHS Tanker freight rates have soared to record highs as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to ?seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America. Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East. Lifting the sanctions on the tankers that are mostly old and not well maintained is “unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months,” it said in the note. Easing the restrictions “could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs,” in the waterway between Iran and Oman. Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said. October 15, 2026 Image courtesy Shipnext Belgium-based Shipnext has introduced business networking capabilities to its digital shipping marketplace, enabling charterers, brokers, carriers and cargo owners to communicate and exchange freight information within a single platform. Launched October 16, 2026, the new functionality integrates professional networking with Shipnext's existing freight-matching, cargo and fleet-positioning tools, aiming to reduce the industry's reliance on email for exchanging cargo availability, vessel schedules and freight information. The platform now supports open and closed group chats, allowing shipping professionals to establish business connections, share market intelligence and discuss cargo and vessel availability within dedicated industry communities. According to Shipnext, more than 1,000 chartering professionals have already joined its networking environment. The company argues that traditional email-based communication creates inefficiencies in freight markets, where cargo requirements, vessel positions and schedules are frequently exchanged through fragmented correspondence. Shipnext's approach draws comparisons to the traditional Baltic Exchange trading model, bringing shipping professionals together in a centralized digital marketplace. Earlier in 2026, Shipnext integrated CMA CGM's bookable freight services and schedules, expanding its coverage across containerized shipping alongside dry bulk, wet bulk, breakbulk and oversized cargo.
